sources.locator: Printed pages 337; each bullet identifies its edition and any comparison chapter. PDF pages = printed + 41.

cards.title: Harrison 21e ch. 53 - Fluid and Electrolyte Disturbances
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 21e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Hyponatremia is first interpreted with volume status and urine sodium. In a hypovolemic patient, renal sodium conservation supports extrarenal loss, whereas inappropriate urinary sodium loss suggests renal causes such as diuretics or mineralocorticoid deficiency. [Harrison 21e, p342, Figure 53-5]

Very low dietary solute intake can limit water excretion and cause hyponatremia even outside alcohol-associated beer potomania; urine is often very dilute with low sodium. Restoring solute or saline can cause brisk correction, so the mechanism matters. [Harrison 21e, p343]

Hypomagnesemia can make potassium replacement ineffective and should be addressed. When IV potassium is needed, saline rather than dextrose is used because dextrose-driven insulin release can worsen the hypokalemia by shifting potassium into cells. [Harrison 21e, pp350-351]

Emergency hyperkalemia treatment separates cardiac protection, intracellular redistribution and potassium removal. Bicarbonate is not a rapid potassium-lowering bolus treatment; a sustained isotonic/hypotonic infusion may help selected patients with metabolic acidosis over several hours. [Harrison 21e, p355]

sources.document: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st edition
sources.locator: Printed pages 342, 343, 350, 351, 355; each bullet identifies its edition and any comparison chapter. PDF pages = printed + 41.

cards.title: Harrison 21e ch. 54 - Hypercalcemia and Hypocalcemia
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 21e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Hypercalcemia can cause cognitive or mood changes, gastrointestinal symptoms, impaired urinary concentration and a shortened QT interval; severity and speed of onset influence the presentation. [Harrison 21e, p357]

Low albumin lowers total calcium. The book's correction adds 0.8 mg/dL calcium per 1 g/dL albumin below its stated reference of 4.1 g/dL; PTH then helps distinguish PTH-dependent from PTH-independent hypercalcemia. [Harrison 21e, p357]

Significant symptomatic hypercalcemia is initially treated by restoring extracellular volume with saline; volume delivery must account for comorbid heart or kidney disease. Loop diuretics are not started before volume depletion is corrected. [Harrison 21e, p357]

Hypocalcemia increases neuromuscular irritability and can prolong QT. Carpal spasm provoked by a cuff inflated above systolic pressure is Trousseau's sign; interpret it with measured calcium and magnesium. [Harrison 21e, p358]

sources.document: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st edition
sources.locator: Printed pages 357, 358; each bullet identifies its edition and any comparison chapter. PDF pages = printed + 41.

cards.title: Harrison 21e ch. 55 - Acidosis and Alkalosis
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 21e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: The anion gap is sodium minus the sum of chloride and bicarbonate; a normal gap does not exclude an acid-base disorder. Hyperchloremia accompanying a bicarbonate fall suggests a normal-gap metabolic acidosis. [Harrison 21e, pp360-361]

Correct the anion gap for hypoalbuminemia: add 2.5 mmol/L for each 1 g/dL that albumin is below the book's reference of 4.5 g/dL. A seemingly normal measured gap can therefore conceal an increased-gap acidosis. [Harrison 21e, pp360-361]

Diarrhea causes gastrointestinal bicarbonate loss and can produce a hyperchloremic normal-gap acidosis. Renal tubular disorders are another group; the urine acidification response helps distinguish them. [Harrison 21e, p364, Table 55-5]

Hyperkalemic normal-gap acidosis suggests impaired distal potassium and acid handling, including type 4 RTA and hypoaldosteronism. This differs from the generally hypokalemic classic distal and proximal RTA patterns. [Harrison 21e, p364]

sources.document: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st edition
sources.locator: Printed pages 360, 361, 364; each bullet identifies its edition and any comparison chapter. PDF pages = printed + 41.

cards.title: Harrison 21e ch. 63 - Anemia and Polycythemia
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 21e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Maturation disorders such as B12 or folate deficiency produce ineffective erythropoiesis and an inappropriately low reticulocyte production index despite marrow erythroid expansion. A reticulocyte production index below 2 suggests hypoproliferation or impaired maturation; a value above 2.5 favors hemolysis. (Harrison 21e, ch. 63, p. 437.)

In erythrocytosis, a low or undetectable erythropoietin level supports polycythemia vera and warrants JAK2 testing. This chapter reports JAK2 V617F in 90–95% of PV, with exon 12 variants in many remaining cases; high EPO instead prompts evaluation for hypoxia or autonomous EPO production. (Harrison 21e, ch. 63, p. 439, Figure 63-18.)

sources.document: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st edition
sources.locator: Printed pages 437, 439; each bullet identifies its edition and any comparison chapter. PDF pages = printed + 41.

cards.title: Harrison 21e ch. 64 - Disorders of Granulocytes and Monocytes
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 21e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Carbamazepine, clozapine and several antibiotics are listed among drugs that can reduce neutrophil production. Acute neutropenia is more infection-prone than some chronic forms; susceptibility rises sharply below 1000/µL and endogenous-flora control deteriorates below 500/µL. (Harrison 21e, ch. 64, p. 444, Table 64-1.)

Lithium is associated with neutrophilia, not the drug-induced neutropenia category tested here. Glucocorticoids can increase production and marrow release and reduce margination; epinephrine, stress and exercise can rapidly demarginate neutrophils. (Harrison 21e, ch. 64, p. 445, Table 64-2.)

sources.locator: Printed pages 444, 445; each bullet identifies its edition and any comparison chapter. PDF pages = printed + 41.

cards.title: Harrison 21e ch. 65 - Bleeding and Thrombosis
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 21e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Bleeding history and response to previous operations help judge the clinical significance of an abnormal coagulation test. Mucosal bleeding favors platelet or von Willebrand dysfunction, whereas spontaneous hemarthroses suggest severe factor VIII or IX deficiency. (Harrison 21e, ch. 65, p. 453.)

Antithrombin deficiency is an inherited risk factor for venous thrombosis. It belongs with protein C/S deficiency, factor V Leiden and the prothrombin G20210A variant rather than the primary bleeding disorders. (Harrison 21e, ch. 65, p. 454, Table 65-3.)

Factor VII deficiency prolongs PT; factor XII deficiency may prolong aPTT without clinical bleeding. In mixing studies, sustained correction favors a factor deficiency; failure to correct, including after incubation, suggests an inhibitor, with interpretation guided by the clinical setting. (Harrison 21e, ch. 65, p. 456, Table 65-4.)

cards.title: Harrison 21e ch. 66 - Enlargement of Lymph Nodes and Spleen
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 21e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Hypersplenism combines splenomegaly with one or more cytopenias and normal or hyperplastic marrow. Platelets may fall through sequestration or destruction in the enlarged spleen; reticulocyte production may rise, although splenic sequestration can blunt the measured response. (Harrison 21e, ch. 66, p. 461.)

After splenectomy, infection susceptibility is mainly bacterial, particularly encapsulated organisms and some gram-negative enteric bacteria. The frequency is highest in the first 3 years; about 15% of infections are polymicrobial. The book reports 50–80% case fatality for pneumococcal sepsis in this population, not for every postsplenectomy infection. (Harrison 21e, ch. 66, p. 463.)

Unexplained fever after splenectomy requires urgent evaluation. This chapter recommends vaccination before elective splenectomy and does not recommend routine oral penicillin prophylaxis in its general discussion because of resistance; this is an edition-specific book statement, not a substitute for current risk-specific guidance. (Harrison 21e, ch. 66, p. 463.)

cards.title: Harrison 21e ch. 74 - Infections in Patients with Cancer
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 21e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Colon and rectal tumors are associated with Streptococcus bovis biotype 1 bacteremia; impaired barriers or local lesions can be the source. The infection pattern in cancer depends on the specific immune defect, not simply the cancer label. (Harrison 21e, ch. 74, pp. 558, 562, Table 74-3.)

Empiric therapy for febrile neutropenia must cover gram-positive and gram-negative organisms, including Pseudomonas. Ceftazidime/cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam and imipenem/meropenem are listed regimens; aztreonam alone is inadequate because it lacks gram-positive activity. Routine addition of vancomycin has not improved outcomes and adds toxicity. (Harrison 21e, ch. 74, pp. 562–563.)

The chapter recommends TMP-SMX prophylaxis for cancer patients receiving more than maintenance glucocorticoids, and Pneumocystis prophylaxis throughout ALL chemotherapy. Its prophylaxis section also includes glucocorticoid-containing chemotherapy. These are the 21e statements; the 22e card gives its explicit prednisone dose-duration threshold. (Harrison 21e, ch. 74, pp. 564–565.)

IVIG replacement is reserved for severe, prolonged hypogammaglobulinemia, total IgG below 400 mg/dL, with repeated infections; routine replacement is not recommended. Live vaccines generally should not be given during chemotherapy, while indicated inactivated vaccines can be used, recognizing reduced response. (Harrison 21e, ch. 74, pp. 564–565.)

cards.title: Harrison 21e ch. 75 - Oncologic Emergencies
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 21e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: SVC syndrome may arise from malignancy or benign obstruction; benign causes account for at least 40%, increasingly because of intravascular devices. Lung cancer causes most malignant cases, whereas distant metastases to mediastinal nodes are a small proportion. Radiation, chemotherapy or stenting is selected according to cause and urgency. (Harrison 21e, ch. 75, pp. 565–566.)

Approximately half of symptomatic pericardial disease in cancer patients is nonmalignant. Cytology diagnoses most malignant effusions, but fluid tumor markers are not diagnostically useful; echocardiography is the key imaging test and unstable tamponade requires urgent drainage. (Harrison 21e, ch. 75, pp. 566–567.)

The thoracic spine accounts for about 70% of malignant cord compression. Local back pain is commonly the first symptom, often preceding neurologic deficits; pain worsens with movement, cough or recumbency rather than being relieved by lying down. (Harrison 21e, ch. 75, p. 568.)

Tumor lysis causes hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia and hypocalcemia, with AKI and arrhythmia risk. Prevention emphasizes risk recognition, hydration and urate control; alkalinization is discouraged. Rasburicase rapidly lowers urate but is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency. (Harrison 21e, ch. 75, pp. 573–574, Figure 75-4.)

cards.title: Harrison 21e ch. 95 - Cancer Survivorship and the Long-Term Impact of Cancer and Its Treatment
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 21e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Bleomycin is linked to pneumonitis and pulmonary fibrosis. Radiation lung injury can begin as pneumonitis about 4 weeks after treatment and later progress to fibrosis; fibrosis has no effective reversing treatment in this discussion. (Harrison 21e, ch. 95, pp. 738–739, Table 95-2.)

Anthracycline cardiomyopathy is dose-related and often irreversible; trastuzumab-associated dysfunction is usually reversible and is not dose-related. Radiation can cause coronary, valvular and pericardial disease, including delayed constriction 5–10 years later. (Harrison 21e, ch. 95, pp. 737–739.)

Second malignancies may emerge years after treatment: alkylator-associated leukemia commonly peaks 5–8 years later and may follow myelodysplasia, while topoisomerase-inhibitor-associated leukemia usually appears earlier. These risks require long-term surveillance rather than assuming toxicity ends with treatment. (Harrison 21e, ch. 95, p. 740.)

cards.title: Harrison 21e ch. 128 - Infective Endocarditis
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 21e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: The modified Duke scheme defines definite IE by 2 major criteria, 1 major plus 3 minor, or 5 minor. A single positive C. burnetii culture is major; other positive cultures not meeting major requirements may be minor. A changed preexisting murmur alone is insufficient to establish new regurgitation. (Harrison 21e, ch. 128, p. 1026, Table 128-3.)

For subacute native-valve IE, vancomycin plus ceftriaxone is a reasonable empirical regimen. Late PVE, with the valve present for more than 1 year, is approached similarly to culture-negative native-valve disease; previous antibiotics and epidemiologic clues affect selection, and treatment is revised after identification. (Harrison 21e, ch. 128, p. 1030.)

Prosthetic valves identify a high-risk group for prophylaxis before qualifying dental procedures, but routine GI/GU procedures do not warrant IE prophylaxis. The text advises against clindamycin because of serious adverse reactions; good dental hygiene remains important. (Harrison 21e, ch. 128, pp. 1033–1034, Tables 128-8 and 128-9.)

bullets: The cited page covers soft-tissue infection treatment, not the meningitis regimen. Staphylococcal or streptococcal cellulitis is treated with targeted antistaphylococcal beta-lactams when appropriate; MRSA requires active coverage. Suspected necrotizing infection requires early surgical exploration and debridement, with antibiotics selected for the likely organisms. (Harrison 21e, ch. 129, p. 1039, Table 129-2.)

cards.editionNotice: Harrison 21e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: In adults, hematogenous bone infection commonly involves the vertebrae. Back pain is the leading symptom, fever is absent in many patients, and neurologic deficits may indicate epidural involvement. MRI is preferred, urgently when neurologic impairment is present. (Harrison 21e, ch. 131, pp. 1046–1047.)

In patients without sepsis, obtain cultures and, when needed, bone biopsy or pus sampling before antibiotics. The table lists antipseudomonal beta-lactams such as cefepime, ceftazidime or piperacillin-tazobactam with initial aminoglycoside addition, while noting that the need for the aminoglycoside is unproven. Route and duration depend on organism, implants and complications. (Harrison 21e, ch. 131, pp. 1047, 1049, Table 131-1.)

cards.title: Harrison 21e ch. 137 - Encephalitis
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 21e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Encephalitis combines altered mental state with evidence of cerebral dysfunction; CSF typically has lymphocytes, mildly increased protein and normal glucose, but early or immunocompromised patients can lack pleocytosis. HSV PCR within the first 72 hours may be negative and become positive 1–3 days later. (Harrison 21e, ch. 137, pp. 1094–1095.)

HSV can produce frontotemporal imaging abnormalities and periodic temporal EEG discharges over slow or low-amplitude background activity. A normal MRI or an early negative PCR reduces certainty but does not exclude disease; repeat testing is warranted when suspicion remains high and no alternative diagnosis is established. (Harrison 21e, ch. 137, pp. 1095–1096, Table 137-2.)

cards.title: Harrison 21e ch. 138 - Acute Meningitis
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 21e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Typical bacterial meningitis CSF shows neutrophilic pleocytosis, protein above 45 mg/dL and glucose below 40 mg/dL or a CSF/serum glucose ratio below 0.4. If imaging delays LP, obtain blood cultures and start treatment rather than waiting. (Harrison 21e, ch. 138, p. 1103, Table 138-2.)

The empiric approach includes dexamethasone, a cephalosporin and vancomycin, plus acyclovir while HSV remains in the differential. Ampicillin covers Listeria in adults over 55 or with impaired cell-mediated immunity. Dexamethasone ideally starts 20 minutes before, or no later than with, the first antibiotic dose. (Harrison 21e, ch. 138, pp. 1103–1105, Table 138-1.)

cards.editionNotice: Harrison 21e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.

bullets: Hypocalcemia prolongs the ST portion of QT, while hypercalcemia shortens it. Hypokalemia, several drugs and hypothermia can prolong repolarization; intracranial bleeding, especially subarachnoid hemorrhage, can cause deep broad T-wave inversion and QT prolongation. (Harrison 21e, ch. 240, p. 1830.)

Beat-to-beat electrical alternans with sinus tachycardia is relatively specific for pericardial effusion, usually with tamponade. Low voltage has several causes, so interpret it with the complete tracing and clinical findings. (Harrison 21e, ch. 240, p. 1830.)

cards.title: Harrison 21e ch. 264 - Mitral Regurgitation
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 21e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.

bullets: Chronic severe MR often produces a soft, absent or obscured S1, an apical holosystolic murmur radiating toward the axilla, and wide physiologic S2 splitting. Acute severe MR may instead produce a short early systolic decrescendo murmur because left-atrial pressure rises rapidly. (Harrison 21e, ch. 264, p. 1996.)

The direction of MR radiation varies with the affected leaflet; posterior-leaflet prolapse can direct the jet anteriorly and mimic AS. Chronic MR unrelated to MVP increases with handgrip and decreases with Valsalva strain. Echocardiography defines mechanism and severity when bedside findings suggest MR. (Harrison 21e, ch. 264, pp. 1996–1997.)

cards.title: Harrison 21e ch. 275 - ST-Segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 21e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Troponin reflects myocardial injury and its time course matters; this edition says cTnI and cTnT may remain elevated for 7–10 days after STEMI. Reperfusion decisions are based on clinical and ECG evidence before laboratory results return. (Harrison 21e, ch. 275, pp. 2055–2056.)

Timely reperfusion is central to limiting infarction. Aspirin, P2Y12 inhibition and anticoagulant strategies support artery patency but entail bleeding tradeoffs; therapy is selected alongside reperfusion and hemodynamic status. (Harrison 21e, ch. 275, pp. 2060–2061.)

RV infarction may accompany inferior MI with raised JVP, clear lungs and hypotension; right-sided leads, particularly V4R, help detect it. Isolated ventricular premature beats do not warrant prophylactic antiarrhythmics; beta blockers reduce ectopy and VF risk when appropriate. (Harrison 21e, ch. 275, pp. 2062–2063.)

Post-infarct sinus bradycardia is treated when it causes hemodynamic compromise. Ventricular arrhythmias require assessment of persistence, instability and reversible causes, rather than treating every brief run identically. (Harrison 21e, ch. 275, p. 2063.)

Anterior infarction can produce an LV mural thrombus with systemic embolism; echocardiography can detect it. True LV aneurysm complications generally occur weeks to months after STEMI and include HF, embolism and ventricular arrhythmias; a pseudoaneurysm is a different rupture-prone lesion. (Harrison 21e, ch. 275, pp. 2064–2065.)

After uncomplicated STEMI, increase activity by walking at home and outdoors during the first 1–2 weeks, then individualize activity to exercise tolerance. Long-term prevention includes antiplatelet therapy and appropriate neurohormonal treatment, with risk-factor modification. (Harrison 21e, ch. 275, p. 2065.)

bullets: An exudate meets at least one criterion: pleural/serum protein over 0.5, pleural/serum LDH over 0.6, or pleural LDH over two-thirds of the serum upper normal limit. Glucose below 60 mg/dL suggests infection, malignancy or rheumatoid pleuritis; the unit is mg/dL. (Harrison 21e, ch. 294, pp. 2197–2198, Figure 294-1.)

Parapneumonic effusions are probably the commonest exudates in the United States in this edition. Loculation, pH below 7.20, glucose below 60 mg/dL, positive Gram stain/culture or frank pus favor intervention beyond simple thoracentesis. Incomplete drainage may require a chest tube or further intervention. (Harrison 21e, ch. 294, p. 2198.)

Nasal congestion is a recognized adverse effect, addressed with humidification or nasal therapy; mask changes and gradual habituation may help intolerance. Oral appliances or selected surgical procedures can be considered when CPAP is not tolerated, recognizing lower or less predictable efficacy. (Harrison 21e, ch. 297, pp. 2208–2209, Table 297-3.)

cards.editionNotice: Harrison 21e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.

bullets: SOFA evaluates six systems using oxygenation, platelets, bilirubin, cardiovascular support, GCS and renal function. Creatinine 1.2–1.9 mg/dL earns one point. A score describes organ dysfunction and population-level prognosis, not a precise probability of death for one person. (Harrison 21e, ch. 300, p. 2217, Table 300-1.)

Cold hypotension with low filling-volume clues supports a monitored volume challenge; cold hypotension with raised JVP and crackles directs attention to cardiac dysfunction and myocardial ischemia. Static JVP alone is not a reliable fluid-responsiveness test; combine dynamic response, examination and imaging, allowing for mixed shock. (Harrison 21e, ch. 300, p. 2219, Figure 300-2.)

bullets: Pancreatitis is a distributive-shock cause, typically associated with low systemic resistance and compensatory high cardiac output. Hypovolemia instead reduces preload and output; the patient may have more than one mechanism. (Harrison 21e, ch. 303, p. 2236, Tables 303-1 and 303-2.)

Initial volume replacement generally uses crystalloid with a predefined response endpoint and repeated reassessment. Ongoing hemorrhage warrants packed red cells and, when massive, appropriate component replacement. Even some cardiogenic-shock patients benefit from cautious volume when indicated; cardiac dysfunction demands assessment rather than an automatic ban on fluids. (Harrison 21e, ch. 303, p. 2240.)

It specifies insulin after two consecutive glucose values above 180 mg/dL; keep that edition-specific wording distinct from later guidance. Early antimicrobials, source control and reassessment accompany resuscitation. (Harrison 21e, ch. 304, p. 2247, Table 304-2.)

cards.title: Harrison 21e ch. 305 - Cardiogenic Shock and Pulmonary Edema
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 21e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.

bullets: Post-MI papillary-muscle dysfunction or rupture can cause acute severe MR, pulmonary edema and shock; ventricular septal or free-wall rupture are other early mechanical complications. Echocardiography helps identify the cause and urgent intervention may be necessary. (Harrison 21e, ch. 305, p. 2255.)

Diuretics remove congestion and nitrates chiefly lower preload; milrinone directly increases contractility while dilating systemic and pulmonary vessels. Renal insufficiency can require a higher loop-diuretic dose. Historical morphine use is qualified by registry associations with increased mortality. (Harrison 21e, ch. 305, p. 2256.)

Takotsubo is an acute reversible LV-failure syndrome often triggered by stress, with transient ST elevation, some troponin increase and often apical ballooning. Recovery is common but does not imply a harmless acute presentation. (Harrison 21e, ch. 305, p. 2256.)

bullets: Nephrotic syndrome is defined by edema, albumin below 3.5 g/dL and protein loss above 3.5 g/day, often with lipid abnormalities. Quantify urinary protein rather than relying only on dipstick intensity; dipsticks predominantly detect albumin and can miss light chains. Causes include glomerular disorders, diabetes and amyloidosis. (Harrison 21e, ch. 308, pp. 2282–2283, Figure 308-3.)

cards.title: Harrison 21e ch. 310 - Acute Kidney Injury
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 21e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: After cardiopulmonary bypass, AKI may result from ischemia, inflammatory activation, hemolysis-related pigment injury or atheroembolism. These mechanisms differ from renal vein thrombosis as a separate large-vessel cause. (Harrison 21e, ch. 310, pp. 2299–2300.)

Vancomycin can cause tubular injury and crystallize within tubules. Aminoglycoside AKI usually manifests after 5–7 days of treatment, can become apparent after the drug is stopped, is often nonoliguric and commonly involves magnesium loss. The cited table does not give a fixed recovery time for vancomycin. (Harrison 21e, ch. 310, pp. 2300, 2303.)

Granular and tubular epithelial casts support tubular injury but are not always present. FeNa below 1% is not synonymous with a purely prerenal process: early sepsis, glomerulonephritis, rhabdomyolysis and contrast-related injury may have low values, while CKD and diuretics can raise FeNa despite hypovolemia. (Harrison 21e, ch. 310, pp. 2303–2305, Figure 310-6.)

cards.title: Harrison 21e ch. 311 - Chronic Kidney Disease
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 21e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: CKD acidosis may be hyperchloremic early and acquire an increased anion gap as GFR declines; it is usually mild and can respond to oral sodium bicarbonate, with attention to the sodium load. Hyperkalemia resistant to medical treatment is a reason to consider dialysis. (Harrison 21e, ch. 311, p. 2313.)

Advanced CKD can cause abnormal platelet adhesion and aggregation with bleeding, while nephrotic-range proteinuria causes urinary loss of anticoagulant factors and thrombophilia. Bleeding and thrombotic risks can coexist. (Harrison 21e, ch. 311, p. 2317.)

cards.editionNotice: Harrison 21e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Adhesions are the commonest cause of small-intestinal obstruction in this discussion; Crohn disease, strictures and malignancy are alternatives. Colonic obstruction has a different distribution, with colon cancer the commonest cause. Distinguish a mechanical blockage from impaired motility or pseudo-obstruction. (Harrison 21e, ch. 321, p. 2382.)

cards.title: Harrison 21e ch. 337 - Evaluation of Liver Function
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 21e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Albumin's 18–20-day half-life makes it a poor marker of very recent or mild hepatic dysfunction. In hepatitis, albumin below 3 g/dL suggests possible chronic liver disease, but low albumin is nonspecific and also occurs with malnutrition, renal or gastrointestinal protein loss and inflammation. Coagulation factors turn over more rapidly and better reflect acute synthetic change. (Harrison 21e, ch. 337, p. 2555.)

cards.title: Harrison 21e ch. 344 - Cirrhosis and Its Complications
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 21e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: For selected severe alcoholic hepatitis, the chapter uses a discriminant function above 32 and assesses bilirubin response after 7 days: stop glucocorticoids for failure, or continue a responsive course to 28 days. Infection and the broader clinical context affect eligibility. (Harrison 21e, ch. 344, p. 2626.)

PBC is supported by cholestatic enzymes and AMA, with biopsy particularly useful in AMA-negative disease. PSC is assessed with MRCP for multifocal stricturing and beading; its strong IBD association does not mean that every IBD patient has PSC. (Harrison 21e, ch. 344, pp. 2627–2628.)

Variceal hemorrhage is a life-threatening portal-hypertension complication, with 20–30% mortality per bleeding episode in this source. Initial stability does not remove the need for close assessment. (Harrison 21e, ch. 344, p. 2629.)

New ascites warrants diagnostic paracentesis; SAAG above 1.1 g/dL supports portal hypertension, while total fluid protein provides different information. SBP may lack fever or tenderness, and the chapter describes ascitic neutrophils above 250/µL as diagnostic. Antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended at presentation with upper GI bleeding in cirrhosis, not indefinitely solely because of a remote bleed. (Harrison 21e, ch. 344, pp. 2631–2632.)

cards.title: Harrison 21e ch. 370 - Approach to Articular and Musculoskeletal Disorders
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 21e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: In older adults, ESR may be elevated without active rheumatic disease, and low-titer RF or ANA can occur without the corresponding autoimmune diagnosis. Interpret serology with the joint examination and clinical differential. (Harrison 21e, ch. 370, p. 2847.)

The medication table separates drug-induced lupus from drug-induced subacute cutaneous lupus. Hydralazine and procainamide are among systemic-lupus associations, while PPIs, some calcium-channel blockers and hydrochlorothiazide appear in the subacute-cutaneous category; identifying the phenotype matters when comparing drugs. (Harrison 21e, ch. 370, p. 2847, Table 370-2.)

cards.title: Harrison 21e ch. 372 - Gout and Other Crystal-Associated Arthropathies
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 21e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Gout commonly starts at the first MTP joint, but fingers, wrists and elbows are more often involved in older patients or advanced disease. Aspirated needle-shaped, negatively birefringent urate crystals support diagnosis; culture is still important because infection and crystals may coexist. (Harrison 21e, ch. 372, pp. 2862–2864.)

Acute gout treatment uses anti-inflammatory agents such as colchicine, NSAIDs or glucocorticoids, selected for comorbidity and interactions. Colchicine needs particular caution with renal/hepatic dysfunction and P-glycoprotein or CYP3A4 inhibitors; flare treatment and ongoing prophylaxis are distinct uses. (Harrison 21e, ch. 372, p. 2864.)

Acute CPP crystal arthritis most commonly affects the knee, then the wrist. Surgery, especially parathyroidectomy, can trigger crystal shedding when calcium and magnesium fall rapidly; aspirate analysis helps distinguish crystals and exclude concomitant infection. (Harrison 21e, ch. 372, pp. 2865–2866.)

cards.title: Harrison 21e ch. 425 - Seizures and Epilepsy
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 21e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: This edition states that acute seizures at the time of stroke are more frequent with embolic than hemorrhagic or thrombotic stroke. Harrison 22e instead says acute poststroke seizures are more common after hemorrhagic than ischemic stroke; retain the edition distinction when studying the older question. (Harrison 21e, ch. 425, p. 3310; Harrison 22e, ch. 436, p. 3414.)

Medication or withdrawal-related seizures are part of the differential; the table includes tramadol, bupropion, several antimicrobial classes and abrupt withdrawal of alcohol or sedatives. Drug selection in a patient with epilepsy requires attention to this risk. (Harrison 21e, ch. 425, p. 3311, Table 425-5.)

Post-event muscle soreness and prolonged disorientation favor a generalized seizure, but neither is independently diagnostic. Syncope can include brief convulsive movements and occasionally incontinence; the trigger, prodrome, duration and recovery pattern must be considered together. (Harrison 21e, ch. 425, p. 3315, Tables 425-6 and 425-7.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 15 - Chest Discomfort
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Chest-pain quality changes probability but cannot establish or exclude ischemia by itself; sharp, stabbing or pleuritic pain is unusual for ischemia, whereas pressure or tightness is more typical. [Harrison 22e, p105]

Anginal discomfort usually develops over minutes with exertion and improves with rest; pain maximal immediately suggests alternatives such as acute aortic syndrome, pulmonary embolism or pneumothorax. [Harrison 22e, p106]

Acute aortic syndrome can cause sudden persistent chest pain radiating to the back with loss of peripheral pulses; this distinguishes it from stable exertional angina in the table differential. [Harrison 22e, p103, Table 15-1]
A normal physical examination is not reassuring enough to exclude acute ischemia; assess vital signs, associated symptoms, vascular findings and the broader clinical context. [Harrison 22e, p106]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 17 - Headache
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: New severe headache needs assessment for secondary causes. Warning features include abrupt onset, a first/worst severe headache, progression, pain precipitated by cough/bending/lifting, onset after age 55, fever or systemic illness, and an abnormal neurologic examination. [Harrison 22e, p114, Table 17-2]

Giant cell arteritis may cause marked scalp tenderness, pain with hair-brushing or resting the head on a pillow, temporal-artery tenderness and jaw claudication; ESR is often raised but a normal value does not exclude the disease. [Harrison 22e, pp114-115]

Posttraumatic headache may follow head injury or, in the chapter's broader usage, some infectious episodes; it may persist for months or years despite a usually normal neurologic examination and unrevealing CT/MRI. [Harrison 22e, p117]

New daily persistent headache requires exclusion of secondary causes. Low-CSF-volume headache typically worsens upright and improves on reclining; a spinal CSF leak may occur even without a recalled precipitating event. [Harrison 22e, p116]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 18 - Low Back Pain
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Radicular pain often radiates into a leg in a dermatomal pattern; neurologic sensory or motor deficits and reflex changes support nerve-root involvement, but examination findings vary. [Harrison 22e, p120]

Lumbar spinal stenosis commonly produces walking/activity-provoked leg and back pain relieved by rest, especially sitting or leaning forward; the pattern supports neurogenic claudication but is not highly specific by itself. [Harrison 22e, pp120,124, Table 18-3]

Local paraspinal or midline tenderness can occur with several mechanical pain sources; it does not by itself establish a dangerous cause. Age >50, cancer history, trauma, immunosuppression, systemic symptoms and pain unrelieved at rest/night are among the listed red flags. [Harrison 22e, pp120,123,126, Tables 18-3 and 18-4]

Saddle anesthesia, sphincter dysfunction, reduced rectal tone or rapidly progressive/severe neurologic symptoms raise concern for cauda equina syndrome; focused perianal/rectal examination and urgent MRI may be needed. [Harrison 22e, pp120,126]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 22 - Fever of Unknown Origin
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: FUO requires fever >=38.3 C on at least two occasions, duration >=3 weeks, no known immunocompromised state, and no diagnosis after history/examination plus the obligatory workup. Inflammation of unknown origin follows the same workup but has persistent raised inflammatory markers without the fever criterion. [Harrison 22e, p149]

The obligatory investigations include ESR/CRP, blood counts, renal/liver and other chemistry tests, ferritin, ANA, rheumatoid factor, protein electrophoresis, urinalysis, three blood cultures, urine culture, chest radiography, abdominal ultrasonography and TST or IGRA. Echocardiography is not a universal item in this list. [Harrison 22e, p149; p152, Figure 22-1]

Subsequent investigations should follow potentially diagnostic clues; repeated history and examination matter when initial clues are absent or misleading. Echocardiography and several invasive tests have low yield without a relevant clue. [Harrison 22e, pp152-153]

Solid cancers commonly associated with FUO include hepatocellular, renal, pancreatic, colon and breast cancer; other cancers can also cause fever, so absence from the common-cause list is not exclusion. [Harrison 22e, p151, Table 22-2]

Giant cell arteritis can underlie FUO in older adults without typical cranial symptoms. In this FUO context the chapter still recommends temporal-artery biopsy from age 55; FDG-PET/CT can miss disease limited to the temporal arteries. [Harrison 22e, p153]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 23 - Syncope
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Orthostatic hypotension is a systolic fall of at least 20 mmHg or diastolic fall of at least 10 mmHg after 3 minutes standing or head-up tilt. Delayed and very early transient forms also occur. [Harrison 22e, p159]

Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension can result from synucleinopathies or peripheral autonomic neuropathies; diabetes and acquired or hereditary amyloidosis are listed causes. The BP finding alone does not identify which cause is present. [Harrison 22e, pp158-159, Table 23-2]

Heart rate often fails to compensate in autonomic failure, though partial failure can still produce an insufficient increase. Consider medications, volume depletion and postprandial hypotension as alternative or additional contributors. [Harrison 22e, p159]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 30 - Coma
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Coma is an unarousable state, but little outward movement does not necessarily mean loss of awareness. Akinetic mutism may leave a person partly or fully awake but nearly motionless and mute; locked-in syndrome preserves awareness with profound paralysis and often vertical eye movement. [Harrison 22e, pp186-187]

Decorticate flexion classically suggests bilateral injury rostral to the midbrain, while extensor posturing suggests more caudal motor-pathway injury. The chapter cautions that these patterns do not localize human coma precisely. [Harrison 22e, p189]

The pupil light response tests midbrain pathways; corneal and conjugate eye responses assess pontine pathways. The corneal reflex has trigeminal afferent and facial efferent limbs; a deep-tendon reflex is not a brainstem reflex. [Harrison 22e, pp190-191, Figure 30-3]

Preserved brainstem reflexes with coma often suggest bilateral hemispheric/metabolic dysfunction; drug intoxication can mimic structural disease, so examination is interpreted with history, toxicology and serial findings. [Harrison 22e, pp189-191]

Brain-death assessment requires irreversible unresponsiveness and loss of brainstem function, including corneal responses, with apnea and confounders excluded. One absent reflex is insufficient; spinal reflexes may remain and do not by themselves exclude brain death. [Harrison 22e, p192]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 41 - Hemoptysis
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Hemoptysis originates below the upper airway; first distinguish it from nasopharyngeal bleeding or hematemesis. Most bleeding arises from the higher-pressure bronchial circulation. [Harrison 22e, p274]

Small-volume bleeding is often associated with viral bronchitis. Chronic bronchitis can have bacterial superinfection with H. influenzae, pneumococcus or M. catarrhalis; bronchiectasis and malignancy are other important causes. [Harrison 22e, p274]

Life-threatening bleeding is judged by airway/gas-exchange or hemodynamic compromise, not volume alone. Protect the nonbleeding lung, localize the source and control bleeding; if the side is known, positioning the bleeding side down can protect the other lung. [Harrison 22e, pp275-276]

Bronchoscopy can localize bleeding and assist airway stabilization or temporary control. Bronchial-artery embolization is the procedure of choice for bleeding from that circulation; recurrence depends partly on the underlying disease. [Harrison 22e, p276]

A normal chest radiograph does not end evaluation in patients with malignancy risk factors, including age >40, or significant hemoptysis; chest CT is indicated in that setting, with bronchoscopy complementary when needed. [Harrison 22e, p276]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 42 - Hypoxia and Cyanosis
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Ventilation-perfusion mismatch is the commonest respiratory cause of hypoxia. Hypoventilation generally raises PaCO2; both mechanisms usually improve with high inspired oxygen, whereas a right-to-left shunt is not fully corrected. [Harrison 22e, p277]

Central cyanosis affects mucosa as well as skin and reflects arterial desaturation or abnormal hemoglobin. Peripheral cyanosis can occur with normally oxygenated arterial blood because flow is slowed and extraction rises; warming may reverse the peripheral form. [Harrison 22e, pp278-279]

Clubbing with cyanosis suggests chronic right-to-left shunting or selected pulmonary disease. Peripheral cyanosis and acutely developing central cyanosis are not associated with clubbing; abnormal hemoglobin forms also generally lack clubbing. [Harrison 22e, p279]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 43 - Edema
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Generalized edema has cardiac, renal, hepatic and nutritional causes; distribution and associated findings guide the evaluation rather than establish a diagnosis on their own. [Harrison 22e, p281, Table 43-1]

Nephrotic/hypoalbuminemic edema may be especially visible around the eyes in the morning. Protein loss and reduced plasma oncotic pressure contribute, while sodium and water retention sustain the edema. [Harrison 22e, p281]

Dependent edema with dyspnea, raised jugular venous pressure and other cardiac findings suggests heart failure; renal disease may instead show hypertension, hematuria/proteinuria or impaired renal function. Confirm the suspected mechanism with the appropriate laboratory and cardiac studies. [Harrison 22e, p281]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 44 - Approach to the Patient with a Heart Murmur
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Acute severe MR after papillary-muscle rupture typically occurs 2–7 days after an inferior, posterior or lateral infarct, with pulmonary edema, hypotension and an early systolic murmur; a murmur can be absent in up to half of cases. A new post-MI murmur warrants urgent echocardiography, stabilization and surgical assessment. (Harrison 22e, ch. 44, p. 284.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 47 - Dysphagia
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Dysphagia can arise from impaired propulsion or structural narrowing; impaired swallowing can threaten nutrition and cause aspiration. Oropharyngeal dysfunction commonly causes difficulty initiating swallowing, nasal regurgitation or cough during swallowing. (Harrison 22e, ch. 47, pp. 293–294.)

Severe cough during swallowing may indicate a tracheoesophageal fistula, but aspiration from oropharyngeal dysphagia is another explanation. Solids-only symptoms tend toward obstruction; difficulty with solids and liquids suggests a motor disorder, with exceptions. Progressive symptoms over weeks to months raise concern for neoplasia. (Harrison 22e, ch. 47, p. 295, Figure 47-2.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 48 - Nausea, Vomiting, and Indigestion
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: History distinguishes vomiting mechanisms and directs testing: vomiting of retained food hours after eating can suggest delayed gastric emptying, while obstruction, metabolic disease and medications need separate consideration. [Harrison 22e, p298]

Metoclopramide stimulates gastrointestinal motor function through 5-HT4 agonism and dopamine D2 antagonism; it is both prokinetic and antiemetic and is used for gastroparesis. [Harrison 22e, p299, Table 48-2]

An antiemetic effect does not necessarily mean a prokinetic effect. Erythromycin acts at motilin receptors; domperidone has peripheral D2 blockade; prucalopride is a 5-HT4 agonist. [Harrison 22e, p299]

Metoclopramide can cause irreversible tardive dyskinesia, particularly in older patients. Some alternative antiemetic/prokinetic drugs carry QT-related arrhythmia risk; selection requires attention to the adverse-effect profile. [Harrison 22e, p299]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 49 - Diarrhea and Constipation
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Distinguish true diarrhea from fecal incontinence and overflow around impacted stool. In an older institutionalized patient, liquid stool can coexist with fecal impaction; rectal examination can detect the retained stool. [Harrison 22e, p305]

Acute diarrhea lasts <2 weeks, persistent diarrhea 2-4 weeks and chronic diarrhea >4 weeks. Acute infectious diarrhea is interpreted using incubation, stool character, pain, fever and exposure rather than the organism's species name alone. [Harrison 22e, pp305-306]

Hemorrhagic E. coli can begin watery and become bloody after 12-72 hours; enteroinvasive E. coli belongs to the markedly inflammatory/bloody group, whereas enterotoxigenic and enteroadherent strains typically cause watery syndromes. [Harrison 22e, p306, Table 49-2]

Lactase deficiency is a common cause of chronic osmotic diarrhea. Lactose load affects symptoms; osmotic diarrhea usually improves with fasting or withdrawal of the offending substrate. [Harrison 22e, pp308-309]

Chronic-diarrhea assessment begins with history, medication/diet review and examination, followed by tests directed by the suspected mechanism. A lactose-exclusion trial with assessment of response can support lactose malabsorption; persistent symptoms need further evaluation. [Harrison 22e, pp310-311, Figure 49-4]

A suggestive IBS pattern does not eliminate investigation for organic disease. The algorithm includes an organic-disease screen, and suspected IBS with diarrhea may require endoscopic biopsies to exclude microscopic colitis or IBD; these cited pages do not establish an SSRI indication from a brief vignette alone. [Harrison 22e, pp310-311]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 51 - Gastrointestinal Bleeding
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Bleeding-ulcer management depends on endoscopic risk: active bleeding or a visible vessel benefits from endoscopic hemostasis plus high-dose PPI, whereas a clean base has very low serious-rebleeding risk and needs no endoscopic therapy. [Harrison 22e, p317, Figure 51-1]

A stable patient with a clean-based ulcer and no other admission indication may leave after endoscopy with oral PPI; the figure allows a regular diet. Higher-risk treated ulcers follow a different pathway, including clear liquids for about 2 days and inpatient observation. [Harrison 22e, p317]

After ulcer bleeding, aspirin used only for primary cardiovascular prevention should be stopped; aspirin for established cardiovascular disease should generally continue or be restarted once hemostasis is confirmed. Do not conflate the two indications. [Harrison 22e, p317]

Hematochezia usually suggests lower-GI bleeding, but brisk upper-GI bleeding can also present with fresh rectal blood, especially with hemodynamic instability. Evaluate the upper GI tract first in unstable hematochezia. [Harrison 22e, pp318-320, Figure 51-2]

Initial hemoglobin can underestimate acute blood loss; pulse, BP and perfusion help assess severity. Resuscitation and risk assessment precede lesion-specific endoscopic treatment. [Harrison 22e, pp318-319]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 52 - Jaundice
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: First distinguish isolated hyperbilirubinemia from bilirubin elevation accompanied by other liver-test abnormalities, then separate hepatocellular from cholestatic patterns. Review medications and exposures and assess albumin and prothrombin time as well as enzymes. (Harrison 22e, ch. 52, pp. 322–324.)

When alkaline phosphatase rises disproportionately to aminotransferases, ultrasound is the next test to distinguish extrahepatic obstruction from intrahepatic cholestasis. Dilated ducts favor obstruction, but partial common-duct obstruction, cirrhosis or primary sclerosing cholangitis can give false-negative duct dilation; further imaging depends on the findings. (Harrison 22e, ch. 52, p. 324, Figure 52-1 on p. 322.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 53 - Abdominal Swelling and Ascites
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Paracentesis establishes the cause of confirmed ascites. Obtain ascitic albumin, total protein and cell/differential count; when infection is suspected, inoculate culture bottles at the bedside and measure serum albumin at the same time. [Harrison 22e, p328]

SAAG is serum albumin minus ascitic albumin. A value >=1.1 g/dL supports portal-hypertensive physiology; a lower gradient points toward nonportal causes. The gradient alone does not identify cirrhosis. [Harrison 22e, pp328-329]

With a high SAAG, ascitic protein >=2.5 g/dL supports cardiac ascites or selected venous outflow disorders; lower protein more commonly accompanies cirrhosis. Interpret the combination with the clinical findings. [Harrison 22e, pp328-329, Figure 53-3]

SBP can lack fever or tenderness; its diagnostic ascitic PMN threshold is >=250/microliter. Prompt sampling in hospitalized ascites permits early detection. A third-generation cephalosporin is the traditional treatment once SBP is identified or clinically suspected; paracentesis alone is not a universal antibiotic indication. [Harrison 22e, p329]

Refractory cirrhotic ascites persists despite sodium restriction/maximal tolerated diuretics or prevents diuretic use through adverse effects. Midodrine or clonidine are described as adjuncts; large-volume paracentesis or TIPS may be needed when medical therapy fails. [Harrison 22e, p329]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 55 - Azotemia and Urinary Abnormalities
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Confirm true polyuria with urine volume rather than urinary frequency: the chapter defines polyuria as >3 L/day. Urine osmolality helps separate water from solute diuresis. [Harrison 22e, p343]

With >3 L/day, dilute urine <250 mOsm/L suggests water diuresis; osmolality >300 mOsm/L suggests solute diuresis and prompts a search for glucose, urea, mannitol or other solutes. [Harrison 22e, p343, Figure 55-4]

Hypercalcemia is a listed cause of acquired nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, alongside hypokalemia, tubulointerstitial disorders and selected drugs; primary polydipsia and central AVP deficiency are different water-diuresis mechanisms. [Harrison 22e, p343]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 56 - Fluid and Electrolyte Disturbances
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Interpret sodium concentration with volume status. In hypovolemic hyponatremia, urine sodium is usually <20 mmol/L with extrarenal losses and higher with renal salt loss; diuretics, bicarbonaturia and mixed causes complicate the distinction. [Harrison 22e, pp347-348, Figure 56-5]

Low dietary solute intake can cause hyponatremia by limiting water excretion; urine is often very dilute with low sodium. Polydipsia is suggested by urine osmolality <100 mOsm/kg, but low-solute and multifactorial states overlap around diagnostic cutoffs. [Harrison 22e, pp349-350]

Hyperglycemia lowers measured sodium through movement of water out of cells; the text estimates a fall of about 1.6-2.4 mmol/L per 100 mg/dL increase in glucose. Do not use an uncorrected sodium as if glucose were normal. [Harrison 22e, p350]

Older adults with impaired thirst or limited fluid access are vulnerable to hypernatremia. The expected renal response is low-volume highly concentrated urine (>800 mOsm/kg); assess intake, extrarenal loss, urine output and concentrating ability together. [Harrison 22e, pp352-353]

IV potassium is reserved for patients unable to use the enteral route or with severe complications; saline is used rather than dextrose because insulin release can acutely shift potassium into cells and worsen hypokalemia. [Harrison 22e, p357]

Hyperkalemia care separates membrane stabilization, redistribution and removal. Bicarbonate is not a rapid hypertonic-bolus potassium treatment; in selected patients with metabolic acidosis, a sustained isotonic/hypotonic infusion can have a delayed effect over hours. [Harrison 22e, p361]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 57 - Hypercalcemia and Hypocalcemia
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Primary hyperparathyroidism and malignancy are common causes of hypercalcemia, but the differential also includes vitamin-D-mediated, drug-related and other causes; PTH interpretation organizes the investigation. [Harrison 22e, pp362-364, Table 57-1]

Granulomatous macrophages can produce active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D outside the kidney, increasing calcium absorption and suppressing PTH; sarcoidosis is one example, not a diagnosis established by the biochemical pattern alone. [Harrison 22e, p363]

Hypercalcemia can produce cognitive/mood and gastrointestinal symptoms, polyuria with volume depletion, bradycardia or conduction abnormalities and QT shortening. Low PTH in true hypercalcemia suggests a PTH-independent process, often malignancy, while other causes still need evaluation. [Harrison 22e, pp363-364]

For low albumin, the 22e text adds 0.8 mg/dL to total calcium per 1 g/dL albumin below 4.0 g/dL. This reference differs from the 21e page's 4.1 g/dL; keep the calculation tied to its cited edition. [Harrison 22e, p364; compare Harrison 21e, p357]

Initial therapy for significant symptomatic hypercalcemia restores volume with saline up to euvolemia while accounting for comorbidity; loop diuresis is not started before volume is restored. Antiresorptive treatment addresses ongoing calcium release when indicated. [Harrison 22e, pp364-365]

Hypocalcemia may cause paresthesias, carpopedal spasm and prolonged QT. Cuff-induced carpal spasm is Trousseau's sign; magnesium and PTH/vitamin-D mechanisms also matter in the assessment. [Harrison 22e, p365]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 58 - Acidosis and Alkalosis
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Calculate AG = Na - (Cl + HCO3), then assess albumin and the expected respiratory response. The book uses an approximate normal gap of 10 mmol/L and corrects for hypoalbuminemia by adding 2.5 mmol/L per 1 g/dL below albumin 4.5 g/dL. [Harrison 22e, pp367-368]

For metabolic acidosis, expected PaCO2 is 1.5 x HCO3 + 8, with a +/-2 mmHg range. A value outside the expected range indicates an additional respiratory process rather than simple compensation. [Harrison 22e, p367, Table 58-1]

Metabolic alkalosis with PaCO2 that fails to rise as expected can coexist with respiratory alkalosis. The book's example is end-stage liver disease with ascites in a patient receiving diuretics; matching an example does not make every similar laboratory pattern etiologically identical. [Harrison 22e, p368, Table 58-2]

Diarrhea and other gastrointestinal bicarbonate losses can cause hyperchloremic normal-gap acidosis; the reciprocal chloride/bicarbonate change distinguishes this pattern from high-gap causes. [Harrison 22e, pp369,372, Table 58-5]

Hyperkalemia with normal-gap metabolic acidosis suggests type 4 RTA/hypoaldosteronism or related distal dysfunction. Classic distal and proximal RTA generally have a different potassium pattern. [Harrison 22e, pp372-373]

Loop or thiazide diuretics can generate metabolic alkalosis through salt loss, volume contraction and increased distal potassium/hydrogen secretion. Classify the primary disturbance and check compensation rather than assuming a purely simple alkalosis. [Harrison 22e, pp373-374, Table 58-6]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 65 - Interpreting Peripheral Blood Smears
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Interpret a blood film with the clinical history and automated counts. Platelet clumping can make an automated platelet count falsely low; a visible aggregate alone cannot establish thrombocytosis. [Harrison 22e, p437]

Iron deficiency can produce microcytosis, hypochromia and substantial variation in red-cell size and shape; thalassemic microcytes are often more uniformly small. Mixed deficiencies can leave the mean MCV deceptively normal. [Harrison 22e, pp437-438]

Echinocytes have small evenly spaced projections and occur with renal failure/severe uremia, but can also be an artifact; acanthocyte projections are irregular. Target cells and Howell-Jolly bodies represent different morphologies and mechanisms. [Harrison 22e, pp437,440, Figure 65-16]

Neutrophil hypersegmentation, with more than five lobes, suggests megaloblastic anemia; toxic changes and Dohle bodies instead support inflammation/infection. Morphology complements, rather than substitutes for, the reticulocyte and biochemical assessment. [Harrison 22e, pp442-443]

Giant platelets together with a markedly increased platelet count can occur in myeloproliferative disorders, especially primary thrombocythemia. A platelet aggregate alone is different from a measured high platelet count. [Harrison 22e, p441, Figure 65-23; p437]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 66 - Anemia and Polycythemia
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Anemia is classified by production response as well as MCV. A low absolute reticulocyte response suggests impaired production, while a high response raises hemorrhage or hemolysis; morphology and clinical context direct the next tests. [Harrison 22e, pp449-451, Figure 66-17]

Macrocytosis is not synonymous with B12 deficiency. Oval macrocytes suggest megaloblastic processes, whereas hypothyroidism, alcohol/liver disease and reticulocytosis are among causes of round macrocytes. [Harrison 22e, p449, Table 66-4]

Ferritin reflects iron stores but is also an acute-phase reactant. Transferrin saturation is calculated from serum iron divided by TIBC and is a different measurement from total transferrin concentration. [Harrison 22e, p449]

Inflammation can blunt erythropoietin production and raise hepcidin, restricting iron absorption and release from stores; renal disease also impairs EPO production. Anemia in older adults is often multifactorial. [Harrison 22e, p450]

In persistent erythrocytosis, assess prior counts, hypoxia and serum EPO. Low EPO supports PV and prompts JAK2 evaluation; raised EPO directs assessment toward hypoxic or autonomous secondary stimulation. [Harrison 22e, pp451-452, Figure 66-18]

Renal artery stenosis, renal cysts and EPO-producing tumours are listed among secondary erythrocytosis causes; this differs from the usual EPO-deficient anemia of renal failure. [Harrison 22e, pp451-452]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 67 - Disorders of Granulocytes and Monocytes
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Neutrophil counts reflect production, marrow release, margination and tissue movement; an increase can occur without a new infection. Glucocorticoids, epinephrine and G-CSF affect these processes differently. [Harrison 22e, pp454,456,458]

Carbamazepine is among the drugs listed under reduced neutrophil production. Drug-induced neutropenia can also involve immune destruction; the medication and exposure history matters. [Harrison 22e, p457, Table 67-1]

Lithium appears in the neutrophilia list, unlike the characteristic neutropenia-producing drugs tested in the linked questions. This is an association in the source table, not a guarantee against every rare adverse effect. [Harrison 22e, p458, Table 67-2]

Susceptibility to infection rises substantially as neutrophil counts fall; ANC <500/microliter impairs control of endogenous flora, and <200/microliter can blunt the local inflammatory response. [Harrison 22e, p456]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 69 - Bleeding and Thrombosis
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Antithrombin inhibits thrombin and other activated coagulation factors; inherited deficiency predisposes to venous thromboembolism. This differs from deficiencies of procoagulant factors that primarily cause bleeding. [Harrison 22e, pp470,473]

Factor VII is assessed by PT; its deficiency can produce prolonged PT with normal aPTT. Factors in the common pathway, such as II, V and X, can affect both tests. [Harrison 22e, pp474-475, Figure 69-6 and Table 69-3]

Factor XII, prekallikrein and high-molecular-weight kininogen deficiencies may prolong aPTT without clinical bleeding. A striking laboratory abnormality is therefore not automatically a bleeding-risk estimate. [Harrison 22e, p475, Table 69-3]

Clinical bleeding history and prior hemostatic challenges guide testing. Mixing studies help separate factor deficiency from inhibitors, with incubation sometimes needed for a time-dependent inhibitor. [Harrison 22e, pp472,474-475]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 70 - Enlargement of Lymph Nodes and Spleen
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: The spleen filters damaged red cells and removes inclusions such as Howell-Jolly nuclear remnants. Such inclusions can suggest absent or impaired splenic function; they do not independently prove which operation was performed. [Harrison 22e, pp479,482]

Hypersplenism can produce one or more cytopenias, including thrombocytopenia, with an enlarged spleen and preserved or increased marrow production; sequestration and destruction contribute. [Harrison 22e, p480]

Loss of splenic clearance increases susceptibility particularly to encapsulated bacteria, including pneumococci, H. influenzae and some gram-negative enteric organisms. This chapter reports highest infection frequency during the first 3 years and about 15% polymicrobial infections. [Harrison 22e, p482]

The chapter reports pneumococcal-sepsis case fatality of 50%-80% after splenectomy, stresses vaccination and prompt evaluation of unexplained fever, and advises against routine oral-penicillin prophylaxis in its general discussion because of resistance. Population-specific advice in other chapters must not be silently substituted for this cited text. [Harrison 22e, p482]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 75 - Prevention and Early Detection of Cancer
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Colorectal screening modalities differ in sensitivity, burden, false positives and the need for follow-up colonoscopy; a digital rectal examination is not an effective colorectal-cancer screening test. [Harrison 22e, p517]
At expert centres, CT colonography has sensitivity for polyps >6 mm comparable to colonoscopy; this statement is size- and setting-specific, not equivalence for every lesion. [Harrison 22e, p518]

CT colonography frequently detects extracolonic abnormalities of uncertain importance, reported in about 5%-37%, which can trigger further investigations; cumulative radiation from repeat screening is another concern. [Harrison 22e, p518]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 78 - Principles of Cancer Treatment
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Late head-and-neck radiation injury can include cataracts and retinal damage with blindness. Immediate mucosal or marrow toxicity differs from late vascular injury and secondary malignancy; normal tissues differ in radiosensitivity. (Harrison 22e, ch. 78, p. 554.)

Small-cell lung carcinoma is listed among advanced cancers with possible cure from cytotoxic therapy; multimodal treatment may still be required. Curative potential is distinct from palliative response. (Harrison 22e, ch. 78, pp. 556, 558, Table 78-3.)

Imatinib inhibits BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase; rituximab targets CD20, trastuzumab targets HER2 and bevacizumab targets VEGF. These are specific targets, unlike the broad DNA or mitotic effects of conventional cytotoxic agents. (Harrison 22e, ch. 78, pp. 558–559, 561, 567.)

Doxorubicin can cause acute atrial or ventricular arrhythmias and cumulative cardiomyopathy. The book associates cumulative doses above 550 mg/m² with approximately 10% chronic cardiomyopathy; concurrent trastuzumab increases cardiotoxicity. Bleomycin instead has characteristic pulmonary toxicity. (Harrison 22e, ch. 78, pp. 562–564, Table 78-5.)

Drug-toxicity pairs matter: cisplatin can injure kidney, hearing and peripheral nerves; vincristine commonly causes neuropathy and ileus, with little myelosuppression at conventional doses. Cytotoxic agents are not interchangeable by target or adverse-effect pattern. (Harrison 22e, ch. 78, pp. 562–565.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 79 - Infections in Patients with Cancer
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Colon cancer can predispose to bloodstream infection with Streptococcus gallolyticus or Clostridium septicum. Infection risk also depends on the cancer, barrier injury and the type and duration of immune defect. (Harrison 22e, ch. 79, p. 577.)

Pneumocystis prophylaxis with TMP-SMX, or an alternative if intolerant, is recommended for adults receiving prednisone-equivalent doses of at least 20 mg/day for at least 4 weeks. This is more specific than treating every steroid exposure as equivalent. (Harrison 22e, ch. 79, pp. 578–579, Table 79-1.)

In the cancer population, consider penicillin prophylaxis for the first 2 years after splenectomy, especially with active malignancy or immunosuppression; vaccinate before planned splenectomy and treat fever promptly. This selected-risk advice differs from the general spleen chapter's statement against routine prophylaxis. (Harrison 22e, ch. 79, p. 579; ch. 70, p. 482.)

For stable febrile neutropenia without a focus, obtain cultures and promptly start broad antipseudomonal therapy; listed single agents are ceftazidime, cefepime, imipenem, meropenem and piperacillin-tazobactam. Instability or a specific focus requires a broader tailored regimen; vancomycin is not routinely added to every initial regimen. (Harrison 22e, ch. 79, p. 580.)

Concordant central and peripheral cultures support true bacteremia; central positivity at least 2 hours earlier can support a catheter source. Catheter removal is preferred for confirmed CLABSI; salvage may be considered only in selected stable patients with clearance on treatment. Hypotension does not meet that stability condition. (Harrison 22e, ch. 79, p. 581.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 80 - Oncologic Emergencies
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: SVC syndrome commonly arises from lung cancer or lymphoma, while benign causes, increasingly related to intravascular devices, account for at least 40% of cases. Facial or neck swelling, chest-wall collaterals and worsening supine symptoms are typical. Metastatic nodes from distant primary cancers account for only a small proportion. (Harrison 22e, ch. 80, p. 585.)

Radiotherapy is a primary treatment for SVC obstruction from non-small-cell lung cancer; chemotherapy suits sensitive tumors. Endovascular stents are increasingly used first for rapid relief, especially severe symptoms or cerebral/laryngeal edema, while definitive treatment remains cause-specific. (Harrison 22e, ch. 80, p. 586.)

About half of symptomatic pericardial disease in cancer patients has a nonmalignant cause. Cytology is diagnostic in most malignant cases, whereas pericardial-fluid tumor markers are not helpful; tamponade with life-threatening instability needs immediate drainage. (Harrison 22e, ch. 80, p. 587.)

Malignant cord compression most often involves the thoracic spine (70%). Localized back pain commonly precedes neurologic deficits and typically worsens with recumbency, movement or coughing. Suspected compression requires urgent assessment, dexamethasone and MRI of the spine; normal plain films do not exclude it. (Harrison 22e, ch. 80, pp. 588–589, Figure 80-2.)

Tumor lysis produces high potassium, phosphate and urate with low calcium; AKI and arrhythmias may follow. It usually occurs during or 1–5 days after treatment of rapidly proliferating tumors but can occur spontaneously. Urinary alkalinization is no longer recommended because it can promote xanthine and calcium-phosphate precipitation. (Harrison 22e, ch. 80, p. 593.)

Neutropenic enterocolitis can follow 5-fluorouracil and other chemotherapy, with fever, neutropenia and right-lower-quadrant pain. CT may show cecal wall thickening and intramural gas, but C. difficile and other abdominal disease remain alternatives. Broad antibiotics and bowel rest are initial measures; complications such as perforation or uncontrolled bleeding may require surgery. (Harrison 22e, ch. 80, p. 597.)

An apical/superior-sulcus tumour may cause shoulder pain radiating down the ulnar arm from local nerve involvement; Pancoast and Horner syndromes can coexist. [Harrison 22e, p619]
