cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 100 - Cancer Survivorship and the Long-Term Impact of Cancer and Its Treatment
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Long-term toxicities can begin during treatment and persist, whereas late effects may emerge months or years afterward. Radiation can cause cardiac, pericardial and vascular injury and secondary malignancies; the characteristic pulmonary sequence is pneumonitis with possible later fibrosis, not emphysema. (Harrison 22e, ch. 100, pp. 752–755, Tables 100-1 and 100-2.)

Bleomycin is specifically associated with pulmonary fibrosis; its lung toxicity is dose-related and DLCO is useful for monitoring. Anthracycline heart failure is dose-related and often irreversible; HER2-inhibitor dysfunction is generally reversible and not dose-related. (Harrison 22e, ch. 100, pp. 753–754.)

Delayed radiation CNS toxicity occurs weeks to months after treatment and can involve reversible demyelination; chronic late injury may appear 9 months to 10 years later and worsen over time. Chemotherapy neuropathy can persist, and prevention of permanent injury may require dose reduction or stopping the responsible drug. (Harrison 22e, ch. 100, p. 756.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 102 - Iron Deficiency and Other Acquired Anemias Due to Decreased Erythrocyte Production
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Low ferritin is the main laboratory indicator of depleted iron stores; the chapter uses <30 micrograms/L as a useful diagnostic threshold while noting that cutoffs vary by setting. Serum iron fluctuates and should not be used alone to diagnose deficiency. [Harrison 22e, p765]

Typical iron deficiency has low ferritin, low transferrin saturation and raised RDW. Inflammatory anemia usually has normal/high ferritin and restricted iron availability; mixed inflammation/deficiency complicates a simple cutoff-based distinction. [Harrison 22e, p767, Table 102-3]

Anemia of inflammation involves cytokine-driven hepcidin elevation, iron sequestration and impaired erythropoietin activity. Normal or raised ferritin must therefore be interpreted with inflammation and possible coexisting deficiency. [Harrison 22e, p767]

After identifying iron deficiency, investigate its cause, particularly gastrointestinal blood loss in men and postmenopausal women. The cause table includes malignancy, ulcers, angiodysplasia and Heyde syndrome associated with aortic stenosis/acquired von Willebrand disease. [Harrison 22e, pp765-766, Table 102-2]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 104 - Megaloblastic Anemias
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Megaloblastic anemia commonly shows macro-ovalocytes, anisopoikilocytosis and hypersegmented neutrophils; MCV is usually >100 fL unless a coexisting microcytic process masks it. [Harrison 22e, p784]

Marrow can be hypercellular while effective red-cell output is inadequate because precursors die before maturation. This ineffective erythropoiesis can raise unconjugated bilirubin and LDH and lower haptoglobin. [Harrison 22e, pp784-785]

These turnover markers do not demonstrate an adequate circulating reticulocyte response; the production response must be assessed alongside the smear and B12/folate investigation. [Harrison 22e, p785; ch66 pp449-451]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 107 - Bone Marrow Failure Syndromes Including Aplastic Anemia and Myelodysplasia
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Drug associations with marrow failure vary in strength: Table 107-3 separates regular cytotoxic marrow suppression from low-probability and tenuous aplastic-anemia associations. Presence in a long list does not imply equal causality. [Harrison 22e, p810, Table 107-3]

Only hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation offers a cure for MDS. Treatment choice balances disease risk, age, comorbidity, transplant-related mortality and relapse; improvement in blood counts is not equivalent to cure. [Harrison 22e, pp817-818]

Decitabine can produce blood-count responses, reported in 30%-50% of patients, while azacitidine improves counts and survival compared with supportive care. Hypomethylating agents can also worsen cytopenias through myelosuppression. [Harrison 22e, p817]

Lenalidomide is particularly useful for anemia in del(5q) MDS but can worsen neutropenia/thrombocytopenia and increase venous thrombosis risk. Immunosuppression is especially effective in selected younger patients, particularly with favourable risk or hypocellular marrow, rather than uniformly in all older patients. [Harrison 22e, pp817-818]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 108 - Polycythemia Vera and Other Myeloproliferative Neoplasms
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Polycythemia vera, primary myelofibrosis and essential thrombocythemia share driver abnormalities that activate JAK2 signalling; overlapping biology does not make their clinical phenotypes identical. [Harrison 22e, p819]

The chapter reports JAK2 V617F in >95% of PV and about 50% of PMF/ET, with JAK2 exon 12 mutations accounting for many V617F-negative PV cases. Thus JAK2 is an established ET association, not a mutation required in every ET case. [Harrison 22e, p819]
CML is distinguished by the chromosome 9;22 translocation; the classic PV/PMF/ET group has a different pattern of driver abnormalities. [Harrison 22e, p819]

BCR/ABL-positive ALL is a recognized subtype and becomes more frequent with age; the chapter describes it in about half of elderly B-lineage cases. A positive official answer involving another malignancy must not be read as denying this association. [Harrison 22e, p844]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 116 - Plasma Cell Disorders
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Non-IgM MGUS requires serum monoclonal protein below 30 g/L, clonal marrow plasma cells below 10%, and no attributable myeloma-defining event or amyloidosis. The cutoff is g/L, equivalent to 3 g/dL, not 30 g/dL. Progression risk depends on M-protein amount, isotype and free-light-chain ratio. (Harrison 22e, ch. 116, pp. 887–888, Table 116-1.)

MGUS usually needs observation rather than antimyeloma treatment. Severe neuropathy may justify therapy when a causal link to the monoclonal protein is credible and other causes are excluded; options differ by IgM versus IgG/IgA disease. Mere coexistence of neuropathy and MGUS does not establish causation. (Harrison 22e, ch. 116, pp. 889–890.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 121 - Coagulation Disorders
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Isolated PT prolongation suggests factor VII deficiency; isolated aPTT prolongation points toward intrinsic-pathway abnormalities, while combined prolongation has a broader differential. Factor XII deficiency can prolong aPTT without a bleeding phenotype. A mixing study helps distinguish deficiency from an inhibitor or anticoagulant effect. (Harrison 22e, ch. 121, pp. 928–929, Table 121-1 and Figure 121-1.)

DIC can also prolong PT and is assessed with platelets, D-dimer, PT and fibrinogen in clinical context; PT prolongation alone is not specific for factor VII deficiency. Serial changes help distinguish evolving DIC from more stable liver-related abnormalities. (Harrison 22e, ch. 121, p. 934.)

Stable chronic liver disease may have rebalanced hemostasis because both procoagulant and anticoagulant proteins change. Abnormal screening tests alone do not justify correction in a nonbleeding patient, and minor-to-moderate bleeding-risk procedures often need no prophylactic treatment. Infection or renal failure can destabilize this balance; cirrhosis does not protect against thrombosis. (Harrison 22e, ch. 121, p. 935.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 123 - Antiplatelet, Anticoagulant, and Fibrinolytic Drugs
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Clopidogrel and prasugrel increase bleeding risk; this edition describes stopping them 5–7 days before major surgery. Perioperative decisions still require the procedure and thrombotic indication to be considered; this passage does not establish an automatic heparin-bridging rule. (Harrison 22e, ch. 123, p. 944.)

Argatroban is monitored with aPTT but can also increase INR, complicating transition to warfarin. Warfarin reduces functional vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX and X and proteins C and S. Thus a prolonged clotting test must be interpreted with drug exposure, not only inherited factor deficiency. (Harrison 22e, ch. 123, p. 950, Figure 123-6.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 127 - Approach to the Acutely Ill Infected Febrile Patient
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: For empiric bacterial meningitis treatment, the table lists ceftriaxone plus vancomycin and adds ampicillin for Listeria when age is over 50 or relevant comorbidity is present. Gentamicin is not part of that listed empiric regimen. Dexamethasone should begin before or with the first antibiotic dose when indicated. (Harrison 22e, ch. 127, pp. 990–991, Table 127-1.)

Asplenia particularly predisposes to overwhelming infection with encapsulated organisms, especially pneumococcus, H. influenzae and meningococcus. Severe S. aureus and other infections also occur; being outside the classic encapsulated-organism group does not mean zero risk. The increased risk persists lifelong. (Harrison 22e, ch. 127, p. 990.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 133 - Infective Endocarditis
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Streptococcus gallolyticus subsp. gallolyticus is associated with colonic polyps and tumors. Late prosthetic-valve infection, more than 12 months after surgery, has portals and organisms resembling community-acquired native-valve infection; timing informs empiric therapy but does not prove a procedure caused IE. (Harrison 22e, ch. 133, p. 1037.)

Definite clinical IE can be established by 2 major criteria, 1 major plus 3 minor, or 5 minor. A single C. burnetii-positive culture is major; an otherwise positive culture that falls short of major requirements may be minor. New regurgitation needs echocardiographic evidence to count as a major imaging criterion; a new murmur alone is insufficient for that category. (Harrison 22e, ch. 133, pp. 1039–1040, Table 133-3.)

TEE is more sensitive than TTE for vegetations and prosthetic complications, but an early negative study does not exclude IE; repeat TEE after 7–10 days when suspicion remains high. In stable subacute disease, obtain microbiologic evidence before empiric treatment; sepsis or deteriorating hemodynamics requires prompt treatment after cultures. (Harrison 22e, ch. 133, pp. 1040, 1042, Figure 133-3.)

Cefazolin is a listed treatment for MSSA native-valve IE; routinely adding gentamicin has not improved survival and increases nephrotoxicity. Prosthetic-valve regimens differ, and the book notes limited convincing survival evidence for adjunctive rifampin/gentamicin and the need to stop them if toxicity occurs. (Harrison 22e, ch. 133, pp. 1042–1044, Table 133-5.)

For subacute culture-negative native-valve IE without prior antibiotic suppression, vancomycin plus ceftriaxone or ampicillin-sulbactam is described, with doxycycline for Bartonella coverage. Late PVE uses a similar empiric approach; previous antibiotic exposure changes the suspected organisms. Revise therapy when the cause is identified. (Harrison 22e, ch. 133, p. 1045.)

Prophylaxis depends on both a high-risk cardiac condition and an eligible procedure involving gingiva, the periapical region or oral mucosal perforation; routine GI/GU procedures do not qualify. Oral azithromycin 500 mg is listed for penicillin allergy, but the text advises against clindamycin because of serious adverse reactions. This book statement does not alter an exam's accepted answer set. (Harrison 22e, ch. 133, p. 1048, Tables 133-8 and 133-9.)

Erysipelas is associated with S. pyogenes, while hand-foot-and-mouth disease is viral, classically coxsackievirus A16 in this table. Match the anatomic lesion to the organism. cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 135 - Infectious Arthritis
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Acute bacterial arthritis typically yields strongly inflammatory synovial fluid with neutrophil predominance; the chapter gives an average around 100,000 cells/µL, a 25,000–250,000 range, and over 90% neutrophils. Aspiration and organism identification are central; a negative Gram stain does not exclude infection. (Harrison 22e, ch. 135, p. 1055.)

Synovial protein and LDH tend to rise and glucose to fall, but these changes are nonspecific and are not required to establish the diagnosis. Crystals and infection can coexist. Obtain blood and joint cultures before antibiotics when feasible, then treat promptly with systemic antibiotics and adequate drainage. (Harrison 22e, ch. 135, pp. 1056–1057.)

Prosthetic joint infection may present acutely or as chronic pain and loosening without systemic symptoms. Aspiration, culture and sometimes sonication or molecular testing aid diagnosis; contamination and colonization must be distinguished from infection. Management combines antibiotics with a surgical strategy tailored to organism, implant stability and patient circumstances. (Harrison 22e, ch. 135, p. 1060.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 136 - Osteomyelitis
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: ESR and CRP are much more sensitive than leukocytosis for vertebral osteomyelitis: the cited series report elevations in 98% and 100%, respectively, versus leukocytosis in 65%. A normal marker lowers suspicion but is not an absolute exclusion. MRI is the preferred study, especially urgently when neurologic deficits suggest a complication. (Harrison 22e, ch. 136, p. 1062.)

In a stable patient without sepsis, obtain blood cultures and, if necessary, biopsy or aspirate before antibiotics to identify the organism. Appropriate highly bioavailable oral therapy can be effective, but this does not remove the need for urgent initial treatment and complication assessment in an unstable patient. (Harrison 22e, ch. 136, pp. 1062–1063.)

For Pseudomonas osteomyelitis, the table lists antipseudomonal beta-lactams such as cefepime, ceftazidime or piperacillin-tazobactam, with initial aminoglycoside addition; its footnote says the need for that addition is unproven. Treatment must follow susceptibility and host factors, and neurologic deficits prompt assessment for epidural infection. (Harrison 22e, ch. 136, pp. 1063–1064, Table 136-1.)

Three-phase bone scanning is sensitive for periprosthetic infection but nonspecific and is not useful during at least the first year after implantation because remodeling also increases uptake. CT/MRI may be limited by metal artifact; a sensitive scan is not proof of infection. (Harrison 22e, ch. 136, p. 1066.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 142 - Encephalitis
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Viral encephalitis usually produces lymphocytic CSF pleocytosis, mildly elevated protein and normal glucose, but early or immunocompromised cases can lack pleocytosis. HSV PCR obtained within the first 72 hours may be negative and turn positive when repeated 1–3 days later; interpret an early negative result with clinical probability. (Harrison 22e, ch. 142, p. 1112.)

HSV encephalitis may show frontotemporal MRI abnormalities and focal temporal EEG discharges on slow or low-amplitude background activity. EEG abnormalities are common but nonspecific; some patients have normal early imaging and different viruses have different patterns. (Harrison 22e, ch. 142, p. 1113.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 143 - Acute Meningitis
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Typical bacterial meningitis CSF has neutrophilic pleocytosis, protein above 45 mg/dL and glucose below 40 mg/dL or a CSF/serum ratio below 0.4. Glucose below 80 mg/dL alone is not the book's specific diagnostic pattern. Cultures remain necessary even when multiplex PCR is used. (Harrison 22e, ch. 143, pp. 1120–1121, Table 143-2.)

Start treatment promptly after blood cultures; an imaging-related delay to LP should not delay antibiotics. The chapter's empiric approach includes dexamethasone, a third- or fourth-generation cephalosporin and vancomycin, plus acyclovir while HSV remains a leading alternative. Add ampicillin for Listeria in adults over 55 or relevant impaired immunity; chapter 127 uses an over-50 threshold, so keep the source distinction. (Harrison 22e, ch. 143, pp. 1121–1122, Table 143-1; ch. 127, p. 991.)

Dexamethasone ideally begins about 20 minutes before the first antibiotic, or no later than concurrently. Its rationale is to limit the inflammatory response triggered by bacterial lysis; starting more than 6 hours after antimicrobial treatment is unlikely to offer significant benefit. (Harrison 22e, ch. 143, pp. 1120, 1123.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 147 - Infections Acquired in Health Care Facilities
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Central-line infection prevention combines aseptic insertion and maintenance, daily assessment of necessity and daily chlorhexidine bathing for ICU patients with central lines. It is a bundle of measures, not routine systemic antibiotic exposure. (Harrison 22e, ch. 147, p. 1148, Table 147-1.)

Measles requires airborne precautions, including a respirator and a negative-pressure isolation room; the text specifies at least 12 air changes per hour with appropriate exhaust or filtration. C. difficile and many resistant organisms instead require contact-focused precautions; soap-and-water handwashing and sporicidal cleaning are important for C. difficile. (Harrison 22e, ch. 147, pp. 1148–1150.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 149 - Treatment and Prophylaxis of Bacterial Infections
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Fluoroquinolones can prolong QT, and combining them with other QT-active drugs increases arrhythmia risk; moxifloxacin is singled out as more likely to do so than other quinolones. Macrolides also prolong QT, so antibiotic selection must consider the full medication list and patient risk. (Harrison 22e, ch. 149, pp. 1171–1172, Tables 149-2 and 149-3.)

Aztreonam covers aerobic gram-negative organisms including Pseudomonas but lacks gram-positive coverage. The chapter permits its use in febrile neutropenia when other beta-lactams cannot be used; that does not make it adequate routine monotherapy. Ceftriaxone penetrates CSF and is used for susceptible bacterial meningitis. (Harrison 22e, ch. 149, p. 1175.)

Macrolide adverse effects include QT prolongation; clarithromycin and erythromycin inhibit CYP3A4, unlike azithromycin. TMP-SMX can cause hyperkalemia, renal adverse effects and cytopenias and interacts with warfarin, phenytoin and methotrexate. Distinguish each drug's risk profile rather than assuming class interchangeability. (Harrison 22e, ch. 149, pp. 1172, 1177.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 183 - Tuberculosis
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.

bullets: A TST induration of at least 5 mm is positive in recent close contacts, immunosuppressed people, transplant recipients and several other high-risk groups; other populations use 10- or 15-mm cutoffs. Measure induration, not erythema, at 48–72 hours, and interpret testing with exposure and progression risk. (Harrison 22e, ch. 183, pp. 1401–1402, Table 183-5.)

Exclude active TB before preventive treatment; otherwise treatment may be inadequate and select resistance. Some high-risk exposed people qualify despite a negative test. Regimen choice must account for the source strain, drug interactions, liver risk and adherence; patients at hepatotoxicity risk require monitoring. (Harrison 22e, ch. 183, pp. 1402–1403, Table 183-6.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 246 - Physical Examination of the Cardiovascular System
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Interpret cardiac findings in clinical context and use a consistent examination and blood-pressure technique; bedside signs guide further testing but do not replace imaging when structural disease is suspected. (Harrison 22e, ch. 246, pp. 1859, 1862.)

Pulsus paradoxus is an inspiratory systolic-pressure fall greater than 10 mmHg. Besides tamponade, it can occur with severe obstructive lung disease, massive PE, hemorrhagic shock or tension pneumothorax; it is not specific to pericardial disease. (Harrison 22e, ch. 246, p. 1863.)

S3 occurs during rapid ventricular filling; a right-sided S3 becomes louder with inspiration. HOCM is among midsystolic murmurs, with obstruction intensified by reduced preload; the murmur becomes louder with Valsalva strain or standing and softer with squatting. (Harrison 22e, ch. 246, p. 1865.)

MVP usually produces a late systolic murmur, sometimes preceded by a nonejection click. With Valsalva strain or standing, prolapse begins earlier, so the murmur becomes longer and often louder; squatting delays the click and shortens the murmur. Most other murmurs diminish with Valsalva strain. (Harrison 22e, ch. 246, pp. 1866–1867, Figure 246-6 and Table 246-1.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 247 - Electrocardiography
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Emphysema commonly produces low voltage and poor precordial R-wave progression rather than the classic tall right-precordial R of RV hypertrophy. LV hypertrophy may produce tall left-precordial voltage with lateral ST depression/T-wave inversion, but ECG voltage has both false positives and false negatives. (Harrison 22e, ch. 247, pp. 1870–1871.)

Hypokalemia can cause prominent U waves and prolonged repolarization; several drugs, including amiodarone, can produce similar repolarization changes. Hypocalcemia prolongs the ST component of QT, whereas hypercalcemia shortens it. (Harrison 22e, ch. 247, pp. 1870, 1874–1875, Figures 247-15 and 247-16.)

Intracranial bleeding, especially subarachnoid hemorrhage, may cause deep broad T-wave inversions and prolonged QT. Electrical alternans with sinus tachycardia and low voltage strongly suggests a pericardial effusion, often with tamponade, but sensitivity is limited. Neither ECG pattern alone establishes the underlying diagnosis. (Harrison 22e, ch. 247, pp. 1874–1875, Figures 247-15 and 247-17.)

cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.

bullets: AF is characterized by disorganized atrial activity, absent organized P waves and an irregular ventricular response. This edition gives prevalence around 20% in people over 80, distinct from the older exam's accepted 10% option. Age and conditions such as hypertension, heart failure, obesity and sleep-disordered breathing increase risk. (Harrison 22e, ch. 258, p. 1947.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 262 - Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia and Ventricular Fibrillation
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Acquired QT prolongation predisposes to torsades de pointes, often after a pause. Causes include bradycardia, electrolyte abnormalities and interacting QT-active drugs. Sustained episodes require defibrillation; IV magnesium commonly suppresses recurrence while electrolytes and causative drugs are addressed. (Harrison 22e, ch. 262, p. 1969.)

The table lists numerous QT-associated drugs, including macrolides, fluoroquinolones, TMP-SMX and several psychotropic classes, as well as hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia and intracranial disorders. A single-choice exam answer should not be read as declaring every other listed drug risk-free. (Harrison 22e, ch. 262, p. 1970, Table 262-1.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 265 - Heart Failure: Management
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Acute decompensated HF management focuses on hemodynamic stabilization and decongestion, followed by appropriate disease-modifying therapy. The treatment phenotype depends on EF and clinical context; chronic HFrEF evidence should not be applied unchanged to every HF presentation. (Harrison 22e, ch. 265, p. 1987.)

Sacubitril-valsartan reduced cardiovascular mortality, overall mortality and HF hospitalization compared with enalapril in HFrEF. Evidence-based beta blockers, RAAS-directed therapy, mineralocorticoid antagonists and SGLT2 inhibitors form the disease-modifying foundation, with monitoring for hypotension, renal dysfunction and hyperkalemia. (Harrison 22e, ch. 265, pp. 1988, 1994, 1996.)

Loop diuretics are preferred for congestion; dose needs vary with absorption and renal function. They relieve volume-related symptoms, but these agents have not been shown to improve survival. Digoxin likewise reduced hospitalization in the cited trial without reducing mortality. (Harrison 22e, ch. 265, p. 1996.)

IV iron in iron-deficient HF can improve symptoms, functional capacity and quality of life, with possible reduction in HF hospitalization; a clear survival benefit has not been established. Oral iron has not appeared effective in this setting. Device decisions require separate assessment of residual EF, rhythm, timing and likely benefit. (Harrison 22e, ch. 265, pp. 1998–1999.)

bullets: Obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy produces a harsh, late-peaking systolic ejection murmur. Reduced ventricular volume or increased contractility worsens obstruction, so Valsalva strain and standing can accentuate the murmur; low preload or afterload can provoke hypotension or presyncope. This contour description is compatible with its classification as a midsystolic murmur. (Harrison 22e, ch. 267, p. 2006.)

bullets: Takotsubo syndrome commonly occurs in older women after major emotional or physical stress and can mimic acute infarction. LV dysfunction extends beyond one coronary territory and generally resolves over days to weeks; MRI may show edema without necrosis. Acute complications can still be serious, and coronary occlusion may need exclusion. (Harrison 22e, ch. 269, p. 2019.)

Cardiac amyloidosis can show thickened ventricular walls without dilation and relative apical strain preservation; these findings prompt a diagnostic evaluation and are not independently definitive. cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 272 - Aortic Stenosis
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Most patients with severe aortic stenosis have ECG evidence of LV hypertrophy; advanced cases can show ST depression and T-wave inversion. ECG appearance alone does not quantify stenosis. [Harrison 22e, p2037]
An apical S4 is common with LV hypertrophy and elevated filling pressure. An S3 generally appears late, when LV dilation and severe systolic impairment develop. [Harrison 22e, p2037]

AS commonly causes an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids and a slow carotid upstroke; arterial stiffness in older patients can mask the characteristic pulse finding. [Harrison 22e, p2037]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 275 - Mitral Regurgitation
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.

bullets: Chronic severe MR commonly has a soft or absent S1, a holosystolic apical murmur radiating toward the axilla and widened physiologic splitting of S2; an S3 may accompany rapid LV filling. [Harrison 22e, p2053]

Quantitative severe chronic MR criteria include regurgitant volume >=60 mL/beat, regurgitant fraction >=50% and effective regurgitant orifice >=0.40 cm2. Interpret severity with valve mechanism and ventricular response. [Harrison 22e, p2053]

EF can appear preserved or raised in MR despite contractile impairment; a modest EF reduction may already represent dysfunction. TTE evaluates mechanism, chamber size/function and hemodynamic severity. [Harrison 22e, p2053]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 285 - Non-ST-Segment Elevation Acute Coronary Syndrome (Non-ST-Segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction and Unstable Angina)
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: The chapter's TIMI table includes age at least 65, known coronary stenosis at least 50%, ST deviation over 0.5 mm, elevated markers, at least 2 anginal episodes in 24 hours, prior angina and at least 3 coronary risk factors. Use the printed table rather than assuming that an appeal accepting every option makes each proposed threshold accurate. (Harrison 22e, ch. 285, p. 2107, Table 285-1.)

Avoid nitrates in RV infarction, hypotension, severe AS or recent PDE-5 inhibitor exposure; the table specifies sildenafil/vardenafil within 24 hours and tadalafil within 48 hours. These checks matter even when angina would otherwise favor nitrate use. (Harrison 22e, ch. 285, p. 2109, Table 285-3.)

Cardiogenic shock or unstable hemodynamics is a very-high-risk feature calling for immediate invasive assessment, within 2 hours unless contraindicated. Stable high-risk presentations generally call for angiography within 24 hours; timing is based on risk, not troponin alone. (Harrison 22e, ch. 285, p. 2111, Figure 285-4.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 286 - ST-Segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Cardiac troponin usually remains elevated for at least 7–10 days after STEMI; this is not an upper limit. Reperfusion decisions use the clinical picture and ECG without waiting for biomarker results. Early recognition, resuscitation capability and prompt reperfusion limit preventable injury. (Harrison 22e, ch. 286, pp. 2116–2119.)

Suspect RV infarction when an inferior infarct accompanies hypotension, raised JVP and clear lungs. Right-sided precordial leads, especially V4R, can show ST elevation; avoid nitrates when RV infarction is suspected because preload reduction can worsen hypotension. (Harrison 22e, ch. 286, pp. 2118, 2123.)

STEMI antithrombotic treatment combines antiplatelet and anticoagulant strategies with reperfusion. Aspirin plus a P2Y12 inhibitor reduces recurrent events, but more potent inhibition increases bleeding risk; agent and duration must be individualized. (Harrison 22e, ch. 286, p. 2121.)

Isolated ventricular premature beats do not justify prophylactic antiarrhythmics, which can increase mortality; beta blockers reduce ectopy and VF risk when not contraindicated. Treat sustained or unstable ventricular arrhythmias promptly and correct underlying ischemia and electrolyte problems. (Harrison 22e, ch. 286, pp. 2121, 2123–2124.)

Treat sinus bradycardia after infarction when it causes hemodynamic compromise, not solely because the rate is below normal. Mechanical rupture can occur early after STEMI, while complications of true LV aneurysm generally appear weeks to months later. (Harrison 22e, ch. 286, pp. 2122, 2124–2125, Table 286-3.)

Anterior infarction and impaired LV function predispose to mural thrombus and systemic embolism; echocardiography can identify the thrombus. Documented LV thrombus may warrant anticoagulation after weighing contraindications. (Harrison 22e, ch. 286, pp. 2121, 2125.)

After uncomplicated STEMI, walking at home and outdoors is encouraged during the first 1–2 weeks, with later activity individualized to exercise tolerance. Secondary prevention includes antiplatelet therapy, beta blockade and RAAS inhibition when indicated, particularly with HF or reduced EF; bleeding risk modifies DAPT duration. (Harrison 22e, ch. 286, p. 2126.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 288 - Hypertension
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Hypertension with unexplained hypokalemia raises suspicion for primary aldosteronism. Screening uses a high aldosterone-renin ratio together with an elevated aldosterone level under standardized conditions, followed by appropriate confirmation and subtype evaluation. (Harrison 22e, ch. 288, p. 2139.)

Testing for secondary hypertension should follow clinical clues: Cushing features prompt cortisol evaluation, episodic adrenergic symptoms suggest catecholamine excess, and delayed femoral pulses suggest coarctation. A list of possible tests is not a requirement to order all of them for every high reading. (Harrison 22e, ch. 288, p. 2140.)

Clonidine is a central alpha-2 agonist with adverse effects including sedation, bradycardia, constipation and orthostatic hypotension; abrupt withdrawal can precipitate a hypertensive crisis. Doxazosin is an alpha-1 blocker, a pharmacologically different class, and can cause orthostatic hypotension especially in older adults. (Harrison 22e, ch. 288, p. 2145, Table 288-4.)

The respiratory examination must be integrated with vital signs, oxygenation, exposure history and appropriate testing. (Harrison 22e, ch. 295, p. 2200.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 296 - Disturbances of Respiratory Function
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Asthma commonly causes reversible airflow obstruction with near-normal TLC and normal or mildly elevated DLCO. In contrast, severe emphysema combines hyperinflation and air trapping with reduced DLCO, while pulmonary fibrosis tends to reduce lung volumes and diffusion capacity. These are physiologic patterns, not stand-alone diagnoses. (Harrison 22e, ch. 296, pp. 2205–2207, Figure 296-6.)

A low FEV1/FVC ratio suggests obstruction, but air trapping can also reduce FVC and make the ratio misleadingly normal. Absolute lung volumes require additional measurement; diffusion results also depend on alveolar surface, membrane thickness, pulmonary vessels and hemoglobin. (Harrison 22e, ch. 296, pp. 2206–2207.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 303 - Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Cigarette smoke is a major causal exposure for COPD, which involves varying mixtures of small-airway disease and emphysema. Diagnosis requires airflow assessment; exposure alone does not prove COPD. (Harrison 22e, ch. 303, p. 2249.)

Stable treatment combines smoking cessation, appropriately selected inhaled bronchodilators and other measures based on symptoms and exacerbations. Inhaled corticosteroids are added selectively, with eosinophils and exacerbation history informing benefit; chronic oral steroids have an unfavorable benefit-risk balance. (Harrison 22e, ch. 303, pp. 2255–2257.)

Pulmonary rehabilitation combines exercise, education and psychosocial/nutritional support; it improves dyspnea, exercise capacity and quality of life and reduces hospitalization over a 6–12-month period. (Harrison 22e, ch. 303, p. 2258.)

Moderate or severe exacerbations are usually treated with 5–7 days of antibiotics even without an identified pathogen, guided by local susceptibility and clinical status. Other measures include bronchodilators, a short steroid course and oxygen targeting 88–92%; NIPPV benefits suitable patients with acute respiratory acidosis. (Harrison 22e, ch. 303, p. 2259.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 304 - Interstitial Lung Disease
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: IPF commonly presents in older adults with progressive dyspnea, dry cough, basal crackles and clubbing. Restriction and reduced DLCO support ILD; a basal subpleural pattern with reticulation, traction bronchiectasis and honeycombing suggests UIP. Diagnose from the combined clinical, exposure, imaging and sometimes histologic evidence, since UIP also occurs in other diseases. (Harrison 22e, ch. 304, pp. 2260, 2262–2263, Table 304-1 and Figure 304-2.)

Pirfenidone and nintedanib slow lung-function decline in IPF. Routine immunosuppression used historically in IPF has been associated with harm; treatment appropriate for connective-tissue-related ILD should not automatically be applied to IPF. (Harrison 22e, ch. 304, pp. 2262–2263.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 305 - Disorders of the Pleura
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: An exudate meets any one of Light's criteria: pleural/serum protein over 0.5, pleural/serum LDH over 0.6, or pleural LDH above two-thirds of the serum upper normal limit. Diuresed HF can produce a pseudoexudate; missing the serum LDH upper limit prevents checking all three criteria. (Harrison 22e, ch. 305, pp. 2267–2268, Figure 305-1.)

Pleural glucose below 60 mg/dL raises consideration of infection, malignancy or rheumatoid pleuritis; the unit is mg/dL. Parapneumonic effusions are generally the commonest exudates in the United States in this source. (Harrison 22e, ch. 305, pp. 2267–2269.)

Loculation, pH below 7.20, glucose below 60 mg/dL, positive microbiology or frank pus favor pleural evacuation in a parapneumonic effusion; LDH above 900 IU/L is another concerning feature. Incomplete drainage may require a chest tube and additional intervention. (Harrison 22e, ch. 305, pp. 2268–2269.)

Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax occurs with underlying lung disease, most often COPD, and can be more dangerous because respiratory reserve is limited. This association does not prove that every patient with pneumothorax has COPD. (Harrison 22e, ch. 305, p. 2270.)

cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.

Nasal congestion can be addressed with humidification or nasal treatment; mask changes and adaptation can help claustrophobia. Selected intolerant patients may be assessed for an oral appliance or surgery, which is generally less effective than CPAP. (Harrison 22e, ch. 308, p. 2281, Table 308-3.)

Suitability depends on trajectory, comorbidity, function, frailty and capacity for post-transplant care; age alone is usually not an absolute exclusion, although older patients with major comorbidity can have prohibitive risk. (Harrison 22e, ch. 309, pp. 2283–2284, Table 309-1.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 311 - Approach to the Patient with Critical Illness
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: SOFA scores six organ systems: oxygenation, platelets, bilirubin, cardiovascular support, GCS and renal function. Creatinine 1.2–1.9 mg/dL earns one renal point; the score describes dysfunction and population risk, not an exact individual mortality probability. GCS sums eye opening, verbal and motor responses, without pupillary reflexes. (Harrison 22e, ch. 311, pp. 2291–2292, Tables 311-1 and 311-2.)

Cold hypotensive patients with low filling-volume clues may need a monitored fluid challenge; cold patients with raised JVP and crackles warrant evaluation for cardiac dysfunction and ischemia. Static filling pressures alone poorly predict fluid responsiveness; reassess clinically and with dynamic or ultrasound measures to avoid both under-resuscitation and excess fluid. Mixed shock is possible. (Harrison 22e, ch. 311, pp. 2293–2294, Figure 311-2.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 314 - Approach to the Patient with Shock
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Distributive shock is primarily low systemic vascular resistance, often with compensatory high cardiac output; pancreatitis is a listed cause. Hypovolemic shock instead reduces preload and output with compensatory vasoconstriction. These categories can coexist in the same patient. (Harrison 22e, ch. 314, pp. 2310–2311, Tables 314-1 and 314-2.)

Initial volume resuscitation commonly begins with crystalloid, delivered with a defined response endpoint and repeated reassessment. Ongoing hemorrhage also requires blood replacement and control of bleeding. Cardiac dysfunction calls for caution and reassessment, rather than assuming every hypotensive patient either needs unlimited fluid or no fluid. (Harrison 22e, ch. 314, pp. 2314–2315.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 315 - Sepsis and Septic Shock
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated response to infection. Full SOFA uses PaO2/FiO2 or respiratory support for its respiratory domain, not respiratory rate; the other domains assess neurologic, cardiovascular, hepatic, renal and coagulation dysfunction. (Harrison 22e, ch. 315, pp. 2316–2317.)

Use crystalloids for initial resuscitation, with balanced solutions favored in this discussion and dynamic reassessment guiding further volume. The commonly described approximately 30 mL/kg is not appropriate without qualification for every patient, including those with end-stage renal disease or systolic HF. Persistent hypotension after adequate volume calls for norepinephrine, targeting MAP at least 65 mmHg. (Harrison 22e, ch. 315, pp. 2322–2323.)

Vasopressin may be added second and epinephrine third when needed; ongoing vasopressor requirement can justify hydrocortisone. Insulin is described for blood glucose above 180 mg/dL, and supportive care includes treating infection, avoiding nephrotoxins, appropriate VTE prevention and removal of unnecessary devices. The card summarizes this edition, separately from later guideline citations in an explanation. (Harrison 22e, ch. 315, pp. 2323–2324.)

sources.locator: Printed pages 2316, 2317, 2322, 2323, 2324; each bullet identifies its edition and any comparison chapter. PDF pages = printed + 43.

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 316 - Cardiogenic Shock and Pulmonary Edema
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Acute pulmonary edema needs immediate support of oxygenation and circulation and treatment of its cause; echocardiography helps identify ventricular or valvular dysfunction. Positive-pressure ventilation may be needed when oxygen alone is insufficient. (Harrison 22e, ch. 316, p. 2330.)

Loop diuretics reduce congestion; renal insufficiency, chronic diuretic use or failure of a lower dose can require a higher furosemide dose. Nitrates primarily reduce preload, whereas milrinone directly increases contractility and causes vasodilation. Morphine's historical use is qualified by registry associations with increased mortality. (Harrison 22e, ch. 316, p. 2331.)

Takotsubo can cause acute reversible LV failure with ST elevation and some troponin rise, often after physical or emotional stress. Recovery is common, but acute prognosis is not necessarily benign. (Harrison 22e, ch. 316, p. 2331.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 317 - Cardiovascular Collapse, Cardiac Arrest, and Sudden Cardiac Death
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.

bullets: For pulseless VT/VF, begin chest compressions and defibrillate promptly, resuming CPR with minimal interruptions and repeated rhythm assessment. The algorithm adds epinephrine during ongoing resuscitation and amiodarone for persistent or recurrent shockable rhythm; drugs do not replace early CPR and defibrillation. (Harrison 22e, ch. 317, pp. 2336–2337, Figure 317-2.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 319 - Approach to the Patient with Renal Disease or Urinary Tract Disease
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Nephrotic syndrome combines edema, hypoalbuminemia below 3.5 g/dL and proteinuria above 3.5 g/day, often with dyslipidemia or lipiduria. A positive dipstick should be followed by quantitative urine protein or albumin assessment; dipsticks predominantly detect albumin and may miss light chains. Several glomerular diseases, diabetes and amyloidosis can produce this syndrome. (Harrison 22e, ch. 319, pp. 2357–2358, Figure 319-3.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 321 - Acute Kidney Injury
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: AKI is defined by a creatinine increase of at least 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours, at least 1.5 times baseline within 7 days, or sufficiently prolonged low urine output. A rise from 0.4 to 0.8 mg/dL therefore qualifies even if 0.8 is within the laboratory's reference interval. (Harrison 22e, ch. 321, p. 2372, Table 321-1.)

Prerenal, intrinsic and obstructive mechanisms often overlap. NSAIDs impair afferent vasodilation and ACE inhibitors/ARBs reduce efferent constriction, particularly relevant when perfusion is already compromised. Sepsis can cause AKI even without overt hypotension, through multiple vascular, inflammatory and cellular pathways. (Harrison 22e, ch. 321, pp. 2373–2376, Figures 321-1 through 321-4.)

Cardiopulmonary bypass can injure kidneys through hypoperfusion, inflammatory activation, hemolysis-related pigment injury and atheroembolism. Naming a possible AKI mechanism does not establish that the exposure occurred in a particular stem. (Harrison 22e, ch. 321, p. 2376.)

Vancomycin can cause tubular injury and intratubular crystal obstruction. Aminoglycosides accumulate in renal cortex, commonly cause nonoliguric tubular injury after 5–7 days and may first manifest after discontinuation; hypomagnesemia is common. Neither this timing nor the table supplies a fixed recovery interval for every drug. (Harrison 22e, ch. 321, pp. 2377–2379, Table 321-2.)

Pigmented granular and tubular epithelial casts support tubular injury but can be absent in more than 20% of cases. FeNa below 1% is suggestive of sodium retention, not proof of purely prerenal disease: early sepsis, glomerulonephritis, rhabdomyolysis and contrast-associated injury may also have low values; diuretics and CKD complicate interpretation. (Harrison 22e, ch. 321, pp. 2379–2381, Figure 321-6.)

AKI complications include volume overload, hyperkalemia, acidosis and uremic bleeding from platelet dysfunction. Creatinine and BUN are functional markers and do not precisely measure all injury or symptom severity. Review drugs, adjust doses and treat the underlying cause and complications. (Harrison 22e, ch. 321, pp. 2382–2383.)

Dialysis is indicated when medical measures cannot control volume overload, hyperkalemia or acidosis, or for severe uremic complications and selected poisonings. Diuretic-resistant pulmonary edema is such a complication; a creatinine number alone does not determine urgency. (Harrison 22e, ch. 321, p. 2384.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 322 - Chronic Kidney Disease
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: CKD commonly causes metabolic acidosis through reduced acid excretion. It may be non-anion-gap early and acquire an increased gap as function declines, and is usually mild; oral sodium bicarbonate can correct it, with attention to sodium load and volume status. Persistent hyperkalemia despite medical management can justify dialysis. (Harrison 22e, ch. 322, pp. 2389–2390.)

Phosphate retention increases FGF-23 and PTH, reduces calcitriol and contributes to low ionized calcium and growth of parathyroid gland mass. Excessive PTH suppression can instead produce adynamic bone disease; treatment balances phosphate, calcium and PTH rather than simply maximizing suppression. (Harrison 22e, ch. 322, pp. 2390–2391.)

Uremic pericarditis is an urgent dialysis indication, but an echocardiographic effusion can be asymptomatic and does not itself establish pericarditis or a uremic cause. Consider other etiologies and tamponade physiology. (Harrison 22e, ch. 322, p. 2392.)

Advanced CKD may cause platelet dysfunction and bleeding, while nephrotic-range protein loss can remove anticoagulant factors and promote thrombosis. These risks can coexist; anticoagulation decisions require individual assessment. (Harrison 22e, ch. 322, p. 2393.)

For CKD-associated pruritus, first exclude separate skin disease such as scabies and address hyperphosphatemia. Moisturization and selected topical or systemic approaches can help; kappa-opioid agonists are described. This page does not establish escitalopram as preferred therapy for uremic itch. (Harrison 22e, ch. 322, p. 2394.)

bullets: The nephrotic pattern is heavy proteinuria with hypoalbuminemia, edema and often hypercholesterolemia, usually with less hematuria than nephritic disease. AL and AA amyloidosis are listed among nephrotic disorders; inflammatory glomerular diseases often have a different urinary and clinical pattern. The syndrome guides evaluation but does not alone identify its cause. (Harrison 22e, ch. 326, pp. 2415, 2421, Table 326-2.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 335 - Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: For NSAID-related ulcers, stop the offending drug when possible and use acid suppression; continuing NSAID exposure favors PPI treatment. Prevention must weigh both GI and cardiovascular risk, and H. pylori should be treated when present. (Harrison 22e, ch. 335, pp. 2530–2531, Tables 335-6 and 335-7.)

Recurrent ulceration can occur at the anastomosis after partial gastric resection; causes include incomplete vagotomy, inadequate drainage, retained antrum, NSAIDs and persistent H. pylori. Distinguish this from dumping, which typically causes GI and vasomotor symptoms soon after meals, or later hypoglycemic symptoms. (Harrison 22e, ch. 335, p. 2533.)

Fecal calprotectin and lactoferrin help detect intestinal inflammation and distinguish it from functional symptoms, but they do not alone identify the IBD subtype; diagnosis combines clinical findings, exclusion of infection, endoscopy and histology. The antibody alone is not definitive; alternative viral, drug-related, cholestatic and metabolic causes require appropriate evaluation. (Harrison 22e, ch. 347, p. 2630, Table 347-3.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 348 - Evaluation of Liver Function
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Albumin has an 18–20-day half-life, so a substantial reduction is less consistent with an isolated very recent hepatic illness. Albumin below 3 g/dL in hepatitis raises possible chronic disease, but renal/GI protein loss, malnutrition and inflammation are alternatives. (Harrison 22e, ch. 348, p. 2635.)

Coagulation factors have shorter half-lives and PT can better reflect acute synthetic dysfunction, though vitamin K deficiency and other causes also prolong it. Interpret a panel and its trend rather than using any one test as a complete diagnosis; chronic hepatocellular disease often lowers albumin. (Harrison 22e, ch. 348, pp. 2636–2637, Table 348-1.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 353 - Alcohol-Associated Liver Disease
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Alcohol-associated hepatitis is a clinical syndrome requiring the appropriate sustained exposure and laboratory/clinical pattern, not merely a recent binge. Severity assessment uses the Maddrey function, 4.6 × PT prolongation above control in seconds + bilirubin in mg/dL, or MELD. (Harrison 22e, ch. 353, pp. 2698–2699.)

The algorithm identifies severe disease as MDF at least 32 or MELD above 20. Eligible patients without contraindications may receive prednisolone, with response assessed at day 7 using Lille; stop for nonresponse, while responders complete 28 days. Treat infection and other contraindications and provide abstinence and nutritional support. (Harrison 22e, ch. 353, pp. 2699–2700, Figure 353-1.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 355 - Cirrhosis and Its Complications
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: In the severe alcohol-associated-hepatitis discussion, glucocorticoids are reserved for appropriate severe cases; failure of bilirubin to improve after 7 days predicts failure and supports stopping, while a favorable response supports a 28-day course. A steroid decision requires more than alcohol exposure alone. (Harrison 22e, ch. 355, pp. 2709–2710.)

Cholestatic enzymes with pruritus and antimitochondrial antibodies support PBC; biopsy is particularly important when AMA is negative. PSC instead requires cholangiographic assessment, usually MRCP initially, looking for multifocal strictures and beading; associated IBD is common. (Harrison 22e, ch. 355, pp. 2711–2712.)

Variceal hemorrhage is life-threatening; this chapter gives 20–30% mortality per episode. Acute management combines resuscitation, vasoactive therapy such as somatostatin/octreotide, antibiotic prophylaxis and endoscopic control. Prophylaxis at presentation with an upper GI bleed is not an instruction for indefinite antibiotics after a remote bleed. (Harrison 22e, ch. 355, pp. 2713–2714, 2716.)

New ascites warrants diagnostic paracentesis with albumin, protein, differential cell count and culture. SAAG above 1.1 g/dL supports portal hypertension; ascitic total protein answers a different question. Sodium restriction and diuretics are used according to severity, with large-volume paracentesis or selected TIPS/transplant assessment for refractory disease. (Harrison 22e, ch. 355, pp. 2715–2716, Figure 355-5.)

SBP may occur without fever or tenderness. The chapter diagnoses it from ascitic neutrophils above 250/µL and describes third-generation cephalosporin treatment with albumin in appropriate cases. Diagnostic tapping itself does not establish that every patient needs antibiotics; interpret the fluid and clinical indication. (Harrison 22e, ch. 355, p. 2716.)

Antiphospholipid testing includes lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I antibodies, interpreted with the clinical picture and persistence. Thrombocytopenia does not exclude a prothrombotic disorder. (Harrison 22e, ch. 369, pp. 2837–2838, Tables 369-1 and 369-2.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 370 - Rheumatoid Arthritis
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: RA typically involves wrists, MCP and PIP joints; DIP symptoms in a person with RA are usually due to coexisting osteoarthritis rather than rheumatoid inflammation. The distribution should prompt reassessment of the explanation for the symptoms. (Harrison 22e, ch. 370, p. 2839.)

RA is associated with a two- to fourfold increased lymphoma risk, with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma the commonest histology described. Higher disease activity is associated with higher risk. (Harrison 22e, ch. 370, p. 2841.)

RF is useful but lacks high specificity: it occurs with other autoimmune diseases, chronic infections and at low levels in some healthy people. Anti-CCP has similar sensitivity but specificity approaching 95%; neither antibody replaces a compatible clinical assessment. Treatment-related infection risk is another reason to interpret abnormal findings in context. (Harrison 22e, ch. 370, pp. 2847, 2851.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 382 - Approach to Articular and Musculoskeletal Disorders
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: all candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Articular disease tends to limit both active and passive movement and can cause diffuse pain, effusion or deformity. Periarticular disease more often produces focal tenderness and pain with active movement while passive movement is relatively preserved. [Harrison 22e, p2938]

The strength scale separates movement against gravity alone (grade 3) from movement against gravity and resistance (grade 4), with grade 5 representing normal strength. The page uses grade 0 for no movement and grade 1 for a trace or twitch; assess the actual contraction rather than infer it from a short vignette. [Harrison 22e, p2942]

RF has limited specificity and may occur in healthy people or other diseases; anti-CCP is more specific for rheumatoid arthritis. Order serology to test a clinical suspicion rather than as indiscriminate screening, and do not equate a positive RF with a diagnosis. [Harrison 22e, p2945]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 384 - Gout and Other Crystal-Associated Arthropathies
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: Basic candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Urate crystal deposition underlies gout, but only a minority of people with hyperuricemia develop gout. The first MTP joint is a frequent initial site, while fingers, wrists and elbows are more often involved in older patients or advanced disease. Aspiration helps identify crystals and assess coexisting infection. (Harrison 22e, ch. 384, pp. 2956–2958.)

Ultrasound may show urate coating cartilage as a double-contour sign. Needle-shaped, negatively birefringent MSU crystals support gout, but serum urate can be normal during a flare. Treat acute inflammation with colchicine, NSAIDs or glucocorticoids as appropriate for comorbidities and interactions. (Harrison 22e, ch. 384, pp. 2958–2959.)

Colchicine dosing needs caution with kidney/liver disease and P-glycoprotein or CYP3A4 inhibitors. This edition generally defers starting urate-lowering therapy until the flare is resolving or over and pairs initiation with anti-inflammatory prophylaxis; that is separate from acute-flare treatment. (Harrison 22e, ch. 384, pp. 2959–2960.)

Acute CPP crystal arthritis most often affects the knee, then wrist. Rapid calcium and magnesium reduction after parathyroidectomy can trigger crystal shedding; infection must still be considered in a hot joint. (Harrison 22e, ch. 384, p. 2960.)

Vitamin C is metabolized to oxalate, which is inadequately cleared in uremia and by dialysis. Excess exposure may contribute to calcium-oxalate deposition and arthropathy in dialysis patients; this is distinct from urate or CPP crystal disease. (Harrison 22e, ch. 384, p. 2962.)

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 387 - Periarticular Disorders of the Extremities
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: all candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Adhesive capsulitis causes shoulder pain and restriction of both active and passive motion. It often follows reduced mobility but can arise without a preceding event, and it is associated with diabetes and thyroid disease among other systemic disorders. [Harrison 22e, p2974]

The diagnosis is clinical after excluding other causes; imaging may rule out alternatives. Physical therapy is the foundation of treatment, with local glucocorticoids or NSAIDs used for symptom relief; many patients improve over 1-3 years but may retain some restriction. [Harrison 22e, pp2974-2975]

Rotator cuff tears commonly cause weakness of abduction and external rotation; no single examination sign establishes the diagnosis. Calcific tendinitis is instead associated with visible tendon calcium deposits and may be identified radiographically or with ultrasound. [Harrison 22e, p2974]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 396 - Hyperthyroidism and Other Causes of Thyrotoxicosis
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Amiodarone-associated thyrotoxicosis has two main patterns: type 1 is increased synthesis in an already abnormal thyroid, often nodular disease or Graves disease; type 2 is destructive thyroiditis without intrinsic thyroid disease. Mixed forms occur. [Harrison 22e, p3040]

Stopping amiodarone does not promptly remove its thyroid effects because of its long half-life; the decision also depends on the seriousness of the arrhythmia. Antithyroid drugs are used for type 1 but may be ineffective even at high doses, whereas glucocorticoids are effective in type 2. [Harrison 22e, p3040]

Near-total thyroidectomy rapidly lowers thyroid hormone levels and may provide the best long-term solution when it can be performed safely, especially when amiodarone must continue. This is a context-dependent option, not routine surgery for all thyrotoxicosis. [Harrison 22e, p3040]

Thyrotoxicosis may cause atrial fibrillation; treatment includes controlling thyroid hormone excess and symptoms, while anticoagulation is individualized. Thyroid storm is a severe acute decompensation requiring urgent multimodal treatment. These thyroid pages do not establish the separate citalopram QT-prolongation claim in the linked question. [Harrison 22e, pp3036-3037]

Other manifestations include hypertension, proximal muscle weakness, easy bruising and striae; hypokalemia and psychiatric symptoms may also occur. The table describes a clinical syndrome rather than requiring every feature in every patient. [Harrison 22e, p3056, Table 398-2]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 415 - Diabetes Mellitus: Diagnosis, Classification, and Pathophysiology
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Diabetes may be diagnosed from typical symptoms with a random plasma glucose >=200 mg/dL. Other diagnostic thresholds are A1c >=6.5%, fasting plasma glucose >=126 mg/dL, or a 2-hour value >=200 mg/dL during a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test. [Harrison 22e, p3196, Figure 415-1]

Unless hyperglycemia is unequivocal or there is acute metabolic decompensation, confirm the diagnosis with repeat testing on a different day; an isolated abnormal value without that context is not automatically sufficient. [Harrison 22e, p3196]

In the Diabetes Prevention Program, diet and exercise reduced progression to diabetes by 58%, compared with 31% for metformin. These are overall trial effects; do not relabel them as estimates limited to older participants. Lifestyle targets included 5-7% weight loss and moderate activity for 30 minutes on five days each week. [Harrison 22e, p3202]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 416 - Diabetes Mellitus: Management and Therapies
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Type 2 diabetes treatment is individualized for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure, kidney disease, weight goals and hypoglycemia risk; glucose reduction alone does not determine the preferred drug. [Harrison 22e, pp3211-3215]

In the trial summarized here, semaglutide reduced cardiovascular events and renal disease but increased retinopathy complications. This is a trial finding in its studied population, not a claim that every GLP-1 receptor agonist causes retinopathy in every patient. [Harrison 22e, p3213]

SGLT2 inhibitors can cause genital mycotic and urinary infections, volume contraction and ketoacidosis. Genital fungal infection and pyelonephritis are different outcomes; the linked question also cites the empagliflozin label for its specific pyelonephritis warning. [Harrison 22e, p3213]

Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state combines severe hyperglycemia, hyperosmolality and dehydration, usually without substantial ketosis or acidosis; overlap with ketoacidosis can occur. Initial isotonic saline restores circulation, followed by controlled correction of water and glucose deficits with insulin and potassium monitoring. Rapid correction is hazardous, especially in older patients with comorbidity. [Harrison 22e, pp3216,3219]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 417 - Diabetes Mellitus: Complications
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.

bullets: Diabetic distal symmetric neuropathy, autonomic neuropathy and focal mononeuropathies are distinct patterns; exclude alternative causes before attributing a neuropathy to diabetes. [Harrison 22e, p3226]

A diabetic third-nerve palsy can produce diplopia, ptosis and impaired ocular movement while pupillary constriction remains normal. Pupil sparing is the feature described in this example, not a substitute for evaluating an acute cranial neuropathy. [Harrison 22e, p3226]

Diabetic kidney disease management addresses glycemia, blood pressure and kidney-protective treatment. Cardiovascular risk also requires lipid management; the specific ezetimibe add-on explanation is in the separately linked lipoprotein chapter. [Harrison 22e, pp3225-3226]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 419 - Disorders of Lipoprotein Metabolism
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Assess secondary causes of dyslipidemia, including hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, cholestasis and medications; the lipid pattern must be interpreted in its clinical setting. [Harrison 22e, p3242]

Statins are first-line LDL-lowering therapy. Additional LDL lowering may be needed in established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease despite statin treatment; management of severe triglyceride elevation to prevent pancreatitis is a separate problem. [Harrison 22e, p3250]

Ezetimibe inhibits intestinal NPC1L1-mediated cholesterol absorption. The usual 10-mg daily dose lowers LDL by about 18% on average, and its effect is additive to a statin; adding it to statin therapy has reduced major cardiovascular events compared with the statin alone. [Harrison 22e, p3251]

Ezetimibe is generally the second-line add-on when further LDL reduction is needed; monotherapy is mainly for patients unable to tolerate statins or selected patients with sitosterolemia. Statin-associated myopathy risk rises with older age, frailty, renal insufficiency and interacting drugs, so treatment intensity remains individualized. [Harrison 22e, p3251]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 423 - Osteoporosis
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: A previous vertebral fracture predicts subsequent fractures even when it was clinically silent. Only about one-third of vertebral fractures are recognized clinically; an incidental fracture or substantial height loss can therefore reveal important skeletal fragility. [Harrison 22e, p3292]

Fracture risk reflects bone density and quality together with falls and other clinical factors. Prior fragility fracture, low body mass, smoking, excess alcohol and family history contribute; increasing frailty and sensory inattention also matter. Do not replace this assessment with a blanket rule that overweight predicts vertebral fracture. [Harrison 22e, p3292, Figure 423-3 and Table 423-1]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 433 - Approach to the Patient with Neurologic Disease
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: all candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Asking how objects or concepts are alike tests abstraction. This differs from immediate recall, delayed recall, orientation and factual knowledge, which assess other mental-status domains. [Harrison 22e, p3380]

Compare upper and lower facial movement: lower facial weakness with upper-face preservation suggests an upper motor neuron lesion, whereas weakness of the whole side suggests a lower motor neuron lesion. [Harrison 22e, p3380]

A cranial nerve deficit on one side combined with weakness or sensory abnormalities on the opposite side supports brainstem localization. Neuromuscular-junction disorders instead tend to cause bilateral fatigable weakness while sparing sensation. These patterns guide localization before etiologic testing. [Harrison 22e, p3382, Table 433-1]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 436 - Seizures and Epilepsy
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: all candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: In the table category older than 35 years, causes of seizures include cerebrovascular disease, tumors, alcohol withdrawal, metabolic disturbances and degenerative disease. The table age band is not a claim that every patient above 35 is geriatric. [Harrison 22e, p3413, Table 436-4]

The 22nd edition says acute seizures are more common after hemorrhagic than ischemic stroke. The linked 21st-edition card preserves its different statement about embolic versus hemorrhagic or thrombotic stroke; do not silently combine them. [Harrison 22e, p3414; Harrison 21e, p3310]

EEG abnormalities can support seizure diagnosis and classification, but an initially normal routine interictal EEG does not exclude epilepsy. The initial study may be normal 50-80% of the time in known epilepsy; clinical history and, when needed, prolonged or repeat recording remain important. [Harrison 22e, p3417]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 437 - Introduction to Cerebrovascular Diseases
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: all candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Basilar-artery occlusion with infarction usually causes bilateral brainstem signs, whereas occlusion of a branch more often gives unilateral motor, sensory and cranial nerve findings. The involved territory determines the pattern. [Harrison 22e, p3435]

Midpontine structures account for combinations of facial or limb weakness, sensory loss and ataxia; use the distribution of findings to localize rather than naming an artery from a single symptom. [Harrison 22e, p3435, Figure 437-9]

An early CT may show no infarction, and small posterior-fossa ischemic lesions may be missed. CT remains useful for identifying hemorrhage, while vascular and perfusion studies answer different diagnostic questions. [Harrison 22e, p3435]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 438 - Ischemic Stroke
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: all candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Antiphospholipid syndrome is associated with stroke and may require long-term anticoagulation to prevent recurrence; the dedicated APS chapter supplies the additional hematologic associations tested in the linked question. [Harrison 22e, p3447]

Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis can present with headache, focal deficits or seizures. The page describes heparin treatment even when intracranial hemorrhage is present; this is a specific venous-thrombosis indication, not routine anticoagulation for every ischemic stroke. [Harrison 22e, p3447]

The inherited rehabilitation question cites this page, but the page covers stroke mechanisms, thrombophilia and vascular disorders. It does not establish the claim that a particular early-rehabilitation window is the strongest functional-outcome predictor. [Harrison 22e, p3447]
