cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 439 - Intracerebral Hemorrhage
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: all candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Pontine hemorrhage may rapidly cause deep coma, quadriplegia, marked extensor rigidity and very small light-reactive pupils. Impaired horizontal reflex eye movements further support this localization. [Harrison 22e, p3454]

Large pontine hemorrhages have poor outcomes, but small hemorrhages can permit survival with substantial recovery. The syndrome is a localization clue; it does not replace emergency imaging. [Harrison 22e, p3454]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 458 - Guillain-Barré Syndrome and Other Immune-Mediated Neuropathies
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: all candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: When Guillain-Barre syndrome is strongly suspected, begin appropriate treatment promptly rather than waiting for characteristic electrodiagnostic or CSF findings to develop. Benefit of starting immune therapy beyond about two weeks after motor onset is less certain, particularly after a plateau. [Harrison 22e, p3620]

IVIg and plasma exchange are equally effective for typical GBS; combining them has not shown a significant advantage over either alone. The described IVIg regimen totals 2 g/kg, usually delivered over five daily infusions. [Harrison 22e, p3620]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 459 - Myasthenia Gravis and Other Diseases of the Neuromuscular Junction
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. P005-2026: all candidates.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Fatigable ocular, bulbar or proximal weakness suggests myasthenia gravis. Anti-AChR antibodies are detected in about 85% of generalized cases but only about 50% of ocular cases, so a negative test does not exclude disease; repetitive stimulation or single-fiber EMG can add evidence. [Harrison 22e, p3627]

Aminoglycosides, quinolones, macrolides, intravenous magnesium and procainamide may worsen myasthenic weakness. The risk is relevant to drug selection and monitoring, rather than proof that any exposure inevitably causes a crisis. [Harrison 22e, p3627]

Lambert-Eaton syndrome more often affects proximal lower-limb muscles with depressed reflexes and autonomic symptoms such as dry mouth or orthostasis. In older adults it is frequently associated with cancer, especially small-cell lung cancer; antibodies impair presynaptic acetylcholine release through P/Q-type calcium channels. [Harrison 22e, p3628]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 472 - Ectoparasite Infestations and Arthropod Injuries
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: Scabies commonly causes intense nocturnal itching, burrows and lesions at the finger webs, wrists and other characteristic sites; nursing-home outbreaks occur. Crusted scabies may be highly contagious despite little itch in immunocompromised or neurologically impaired patients. [Harrison 22e, p3729]

Permethrin 5% is a topical scabicide. Treatment usually needs a second application a week later because eggs are relatively resistant, and close contacts should be treated together to prevent reinfestation. Crusted disease may require combined repeated topical and oral treatment. [Harrison 22e, p3729]

This cited page supports permethrin for scabies, not for uremic pruritus. Persistent itch after adequate scabies treatment can reflect hypersensitivity to dead mites; unnecessary repeated topical treatment can itself cause dermatitis. [Harrison 22e, p3729]

cards.title: Harrison 22e ch. 492 - Medical Evaluation of the Patient Undergoing Noncardiac Surgery
cards.editionNotice: Harrison 22e; printed page numbers. Additional cited reading; this edition/chapter is not listed in P005-2026.
cards.provenance: Original summaries from visually read rendered pages of the supplied local edition; coverage is limited to the cited questions.
bullets: For elective noncardiac surgery, the cited interruption intervals are 5 days after the last clopidogrel dose, 7 days after prasugrel, and 3-5 days after ticagrelor. These intervals do not remove the need to assess recent stenting and thrombosis risk. [Harrison 22e, p3908]

When a P2Y12 inhibitor must be stopped in a patient with a coronary stent, aspirin is generally continued unless bleeding consequences would be catastrophic, and the P2Y12 inhibitor is restarted promptly after surgery. Multidisciplinary planning is emphasized; the page discusses limited cangrelor bridging evidence, not routine low-molecular-weight heparin replacement for antiplatelet therapy. [Harrison 22e, p3908]

Continue chronic beta-blocker and statin therapy where appropriate; avoid starting a beta blocker on the day of surgery. SGLT2 inhibitors should be interrupted at least 3-4 days before scheduled noncardiac surgery because fasting and perioperative stress can precipitate euglycemic ketoacidosis. [Harrison 22e, p3908]

cards.title: IWG 2024: AD is a clinical-biological construct
cards.provenance: jamaneurology_dubois_2024_sc_240001_1733257847.6341.pdf – official publisher PDF; journal pages 1304–1311.
bullets: Position: AD = clinical phenotype + positive pathophysiological AD biomarkers; opposes AA 2024 purely biological definition. [pp.1305,1308]

AD diagnosis (clinical setting): established clinical phenotype + supportive biomarkers (CSF, amyloid or tau PET; plasma e.g. p-tau217 pending approval). Covers prodromal (MCI, no loss of function) and dementia (loss of function) stages. [pp.1306,1308; Box]

Phenotypes - common: amnestic syndrome of the hippocampal type, logopenic aphasia, posterior cortical atrophy; uncommon: corticobasal syndrome, behavioural and dysexecutive variants. [pp.1305–1306; Box]

Cognitively normal + biomarker-positive = "asymptomatic at-risk for AD", NOT AD: brain amyloidosis isolated, or with tauopathy limited to medial temporal regions, or positive phospho-tau fluid biomarker. [p.1306, Box]

"Presymptomatic AD" (rare): near-deterministic risk - APP/PSEN1/PSEN2 mutations; Down syndrome; APOE e4 homozygous with SORL1 loss of function; amyloid PET+ with tau PET+ in neocortical regions. [p.1306, Box]

Numbers: lifetime AD-dementia risk of an amyloid-positive 65-year-old man ~21.9%, only 1.7x amyloid-negative; ~17% of CN isolated-amyloid-positive progressed to MCI over 6 years; tau PET positivity ~35% progression at 7 years. [p.1306]
IWG recommends NO routine diagnostic biomarker testing in cognitively normal people (incl. subjective cognitive decline) outside research. [p.1308]

Table AA 2024 vs IWG 2024: AA - any abnormal Core 1 biomarker suffices, CN biomarker+ can be told they have AD, biomarkers could be primary trial endpoints; IWG - objective cognitive deficits + biomarkers needed, CN biomarker+ = at-risk (except rare presymptomatic AD), clinical efficacy required. [p.1307, Table]

cards.title: VASCOG-2-WSO 2025: vascular cognitive impairment and dementia
cards.provenance: jamaneurology_sachdev_2025_oi_250068_1762755358.15855.pdf – official publisher PDF; journal pages 1103–1112. Gait wording checked in Observations p.1106 and Box 2 A.2 p.1107.
bullets: Terms (84% consensus): umbrella VCID; mild level = vaMCI; major level = VaD. Delphi, >=75% agreement, 3 rounds, 49-54 experts; endorsed by World Stroke Organisation. [pp.1103–1105]
VaD = 2nd commonest dementia, 15-20% of cases; cerebrovascular disease contributes in up to 75% of dementia. [p.1103]
MCI (Box 1): concern + modest objective deficit in >=1 domain, typically 1-2 SD below norms (3rd-16th percentile); IADLs preserved (may need effort/compensation). [p.1106, Box 1]

Dementia (Box 1): concern + clear and significant deficit in >=1 domain on objective assessment, typically >=2 SD below appropriate norms (<3rd percentile) and/or below estimated premorbid functioning on formal neuropsychological testing, or an equivalent level judged by clinical evaluation including cognitive screening tests; deficits, apart from physical deficits, interfere with independence (at least needing help with IADLs e.g. finances, medications). [p.1106, Box 1]
Six domains (Table, DSM-5 based): attention and processing speed; executive function; learning and memory; language; perceptual-motor; social cognition. [pp.1105–1106, Table]

Vascular aetiology (Box 2) needs A AND B. A1: onset temporally related to >=1 clinical stroke; abrupt; deficits persist beyond 3 months; stepwise/fluctuating if multiple strokes. A2 (no stroke/TIA): gradual, slowly progressive, mainly attention/processing speed and/or executive; memory = inefficient encoding/retrieval (vs consolidation/storage in AD). Supportive: apathy, depressive symptoms, emotional lability, gait-balance disorders. [p.1107, Box 2 A]

B imaging (MRI preferred, >=1): multiple infarcts or a single extensive/strategic infarct (e.g. thalamus); >=2 lacunes outside brainstem (1 if strategic or with extensive WMH); extensive confluent WMH (may correspond to Fazekas 2-3, or periventricular 3 and/or deep 2-3); ICH - one if large/lobar/strategic, or >=2. Microbleeds, cortical superficial siderosis and CAA (Boston 2.0) are supportive only, not sufficient. STRIVE-2 definitions. [p.1107, Box 2 B]

Changes vs VASCOG-1: gait disturbance and urinary frequency dropped as too non-specific; major depression removed from exclusions; AD and DLB biomarkers added for alternative/additional aetiology; no consensus on a timeframe after stroke ("beyond 3 months" retained from VASCOG-1; 3 mo 39%, 6 mo 30%); PSD / SIVaD / MID subtypes not supported - only ischaemic, haemorrhagic or mixed. [pp.1105–1106,1108]

Box 2 C alternative/co-aetiology: insidious AD-like onset without matching vascular lesions; early prominent movement disorder (Lewy body); absent/minimal CVD on imaging; AD biomarkers (CSF/plasma Abeta42:40, pTau181, pTau217; amyloid PET; AD mutation or APOE4 homozygosity - authors' addition, not Delphi consensus); DLB biomarkers (DaT imaging, CSF alpha-synuclein seed amplification - authors' addition, not Delphi consensus). [p.1107, Box 2 C]

Certainty (Box 3): probable = clinical criteria + neuroimaging, or clinical + genetic (CADASIL, CARASIL, HERNS, PADMAL, RVCL, COL4A1); possible = clinical criteria met but neuroimaging and/or genetic evidence is not available. Mixed causation: state which aetiology is clinically more salient. [p.1108, Box 3]

New "preclinical/at-risk VCID": significant incidental imaging CVD meeting criterion B, no cognitive concern and not meeting MCI/dementia; supported by vascular risk factors; mainly for research and prevention. [p.1108, Box 3]

cards.title: AA 2024: biological diagnosis and staging of AD
cards.provenance: 4_AA-revised-criteria-AD_Alz-Dement-2024_PMC11350039.xml — supplied Europe PMC full-text XML; citations use its section headings, boxes and tables.
bullets: Biological definition: AD is defined by its neuropathologic biology, separately from the clinical syndrome. An abnormal, sufficiently accurate Core 1 test can establish AD; symptoms are not required. A clinical phenotype alone cannot establish AD biology. [BACKGROUND, Box 1; DIAGNOSIS, Box 2]

Core 1 = A (amyloid pathway) + T1 (early-changing phosphorylated/secreted tau: p-tau217, p-tau181, p-tau231), including hybrid ratios. Diagnostic tests include amyloid PET, CSF Aβ42/40, CSF p-tau181/Aβ42, CSF t-tau/Aβ42 and accurate plasma assays. Not every test in this category is accurate enough for diagnosis. [BIOMARKER CATEGORIZATION, Box 2, Tables 1–2]

Accuracy requirement: at least 90% against an accepted reference standard in the intended-use population; qualifying plasma tests should perform equivalently to approved CSF assays. Table 2 emphasizes plasma p-tau217 and %p-tau217. [DIAGNOSIS — Anchoring Core 1 biomarkers for AD diagnosis to reference standards; Box 2; Table 2]

Core 2 = T2: later-changing tau markers, including tau PET, MTBR-tau243 and other tau fragments (e.g. p-tau205). They support biological staging and prognosis with Core 1; a negative Core 2 result does not rule out early AD. Several fluid markers remain less validated. [BIOMARKER CATEGORIZATION, Box 2, Tables 1–2]

Biological PET stages: A = amyloid-positive / tau PET-negative; B = medial-temporal tau; C = moderate neocortical tau uptake; D = high neocortical tau uptake. All four are amyloid-positive. [BIOLOGICAL DISEASE STAGING; Tables 3–4]

A positive Core 1 fluid assay establishes biological stage A or higher, but cannot alone distinguish PET stages A–D; add tau PET to separate them. Fluid-only A–D staging is conceptual, awaiting validation, and is not interchangeable with PET staging. [BIOLOGICAL DISEASE STAGING; Tables 3–5]

Clinical 0: asymptomatic, genetically determined AD (ADAD or Down syndrome-associated AD), with normal biomarkers. Clinical 1: asymptomatic with biomarker evidence. APOE risk alleles alone are neither diagnostic nor a disease stage. [CLINICAL STAGING — Stage 0 / Risk alleles; Table 6]

Clinical 2: transitional cognitive/neurobehavioral decline from baseline within 1–3 years, persistent ≥6 months; objective testing still within expected range and daily independence retained. Clinical 3: objective impairment, with more effort/time or reduced efficiency for complex activities, but still independent. [CLINICAL STAGING — Numeric clinical staging; Table 6]

Clinical 4: mild dementia, impaired instrumental ADLs but independent basic ADLs. Clinical 5: moderate dementia, assistance with basic ADLs. Clinical 6: severe dementia, completely dependent for basic ADLs. [CLINICAL STAGING; Table 6]

Integrated stage combines clinical number and biological letter (e.g. 3B). Biological and clinical severity may diverge because of copathology or cognitive reserve; stage 0 has no A–D combination. [INTEGRATED BIOLOGICAL AND CLINICAL STAGING; Table 7]

Cognitively unimpaired people: AD can be diagnosed biologically, but the workgroup recommends AGAINST diagnostic testing for clinical purposes outside observational or therapeutic research at the time of this paper. Clinical biomarker use is intended for symptomatic people and assists clinical evaluation; it does not replace evaluation for other contributors. [DIAGNOSIS — Intended uses; Box 4]

cards.title: Dementia Prevention and Treatment · JAMA Intern Med 2024
cards.provenance: 5_Dementia-prevention-treatment_JAMA-IM-2024_eScholarship.pdf — supplied PDF, printed E-pages = PDF page number prefixed E. Summary reflects this 2024 paper.
bullets: Prevention evidence: most evidence is observational. The review finds no conclusive RCT evidence that modifying a risk factor, alone or in combination, prevents dementia; addressing risks can still have other health benefits. Cognitive improvement is not proof of dementia prevention. [p.E1–E4, p.E7; Tables 1–2]

The 12 modifiable factors (2020 Lancet model) account for an estimated 39.7% of dementia: less education, hearing loss, traumatic brain injury, hypertension, alcohol >21 units/week, obesity (BMI ≥30), smoking, depression, social isolation, physical inactivity, diabetes and air pollution. This is an attributable-risk estimate, not a proven intervention effect. [p.E2, Table 1]

SPRINT MIND: systolic target <120 versus <140 mmHg reduced probable dementia by 17%, but not significantly; MCI and the combined MCI/dementia outcome were significantly reduced. Statins and aspirin did not show preventive benefit in the cited trial reviews/trial. [p.E2–E3, Table 2]

Hearing: observational evidence suggested benefit, but the cited 3-year hearing-intervention trial found no overall cognitive benefit. MIND diet: observational support, but the 3-year trial found no difference in global cognition or dementia-related MRI findings. [p.E2–E3, Table 2]

Exercise can improve cognition; smoking cessation is associated with lower dementia risk in observational data. FINGER (diet, exercise, cognitive training and vascular-risk management) improved cognition, but follow-up was too short to determine dementia prevention. SMARRT found modest improvements in cognition, risk factors and quality of life. [p.E3–E4, Table 2]

Symptomatic AD treatment: donepezil and rivastigmine for mild–severe AD dementia; galantamine for mild–moderate; memantine (NMDA antagonist) for moderate–severe. Benefits are modest; the review describes persistent cognitive benefit for cholinesterase inhibitors and delayed institutionalization/reduced caregiver burden with these drugs and memantine. [p.E4–E5, Table 3]

Cholinesterase-inhibitor adverse effects include GI upset, weight loss, vivid dreams, bradycardia and syncope; rivastigmine patch can cause contact dermatitis. Memantine adverse effects listed include dizziness, confusion, anxiety, blood-pressure changes, diarrhea and agitation. [p.E4, Table 3]

Anti-amyloid antibodies: for MCI or mild dementia due to AD. Lecanemab/donanemab trials slowed cognitive/functional decline by 27–40% versus placebo; an estimated ≈5-month delay does not establish a sustained, clinically important benefit for every individual. Aducanumab clinical efficacy was inconclusive; Table 3 labels donanemab as under FDA consideration at the time of the paper. [p.E4–E5, Table 3]

Eligibility workup described: cognitive testing to exclude moderate/severe dementia, proof of elevated brain amyloid, APOE ε4 testing, and baseline MRI. One macrohemorrhage or >4 microhemorrhages excludes starting treatment in the paper’s account. Infusions and serial surveillance MRIs add substantial burden. [p.E6]

ARIA-E = edema; ARIA-H = hemorrhage/siderosis. Risk rises with APOE ε4, especially homozygosity. About 70% of ARIA is asymptomatic; possible symptoms include confusion, headache, seizures and focal signs. Close clinical/MRI monitoring is needed, especially in the first 5 months; abrupt neurologic change warrants urgent evaluation including MRI. [p.E5–E6]

Non-drug care first for behavioral/psychological symptoms: DICE (Describe, Investigate, Create, Evaluate); identify medical, caregiver and environmental triggers. Caregiver skills training, psychoeducation and tailored activities have the most consistent evidence and reduce symptoms and caregiver distress. [p.E6]

If distressing/dangerous symptoms persist, consider a time-limited drug trial with objective goals and review ineffective psychoactive drugs before adding another. Psychotropics carry fall and cognitive risks; antipsychotics increase mortality. Patient/caregiver goals, community support, advance directives and hospice also matter. [p.E6–E7]

cards.title: Age-Related Hearing Loss · NEJM 2024
cards.provenance: NEJMcp2306778.pdf - official publisher PDF via owner's institutional library access; printed pages 1505-1512.
bullets: Mechanism and presentation: progressive loss of nonregenerating cochlear sensory hair cells degrades sound encoding into neural signals; hearing declines from early adulthood, especially at higher frequencies. Typical age-related loss is gradual and bilateral without a clear inciting event. Difficulty understanding speech in noise often precedes difficulty in quiet; relatives may notice before the patient does. [p.1505–1506]

Risk factors: older age, lighter skin color (a marker of cochlear pigmentation; melanin is protective), male sex and noise exposure are the strongest factors listed. Diabetes, smoking and hypertension may contribute through microvascular injury to cochlear vessels. [p.1505]

Prevalence: clinically significant hearing loss nearly doubles with each decade; more than two thirds of adults 60 years or older have some clinically significant loss. The estimated US burden in 2019 was approximately 72.9 million, or one in five persons. Figure 1 shows increasing prevalence and severity across ages 20–29, 30–39, 40–49, 50–59, 60–69, 70–79 and ≥80; exact percentages for individual bars are not printed. [p.1505; p.1507, Figure 1]

Evaluation framework: distinguish the incoming speech signal, conductive hearing, sensorineural hearing and central auditory processing. Distance, competing noise and reverberation degrade speech; cognitive impairment, traumatic brain injury and attention disorders can impair central decoding. More than one component may contribute. [p.1506; p.1508, Table 1]

Initial assessment: use history and otoscopy to identify treatable conductive causes such as otitis media and complete cerumen impaction. Ear drainage, abnormal otoscopy, unremitting tinnitus, vertigo, fluctuating or asymmetric hearing, or sudden loss without a conductive explanation warrant further evaluation or otolaryngology consultation. [p.1506]

Urgent referral: sudden sensorineural loss needs otolaryngology evaluation, ideally within 3 days after onset; earlier diagnosis and glucocorticoid treatment may improve recovery. It often presents as acute painless unilateral loss with near-complete inability to hear or understand speech in that ear. Annual incidence is 1 in 10,000 persons, most commonly in adults 40 years or older. [p.1506–1507]

Screening: whispered-voice and finger-rub tests have widely varying sensitivity and specificity. Age, compatible symptoms and absence of findings suggesting another cause may support presumed age-related loss regardless of screening results. Smartphone applications can measure and track the four-frequency pure tone average (PTA4), also called the hearing number. [p.1507]

Confirmation: refer to an audiologist for calibrated audiometry in a sound-attenuating enclosure. Thresholds are tested from 125 to 8000 Hz; lower thresholds mean better hearing. PTA4 averages thresholds at 500, 1000, 2000 and 4000 Hz. Bone-conduction audiometry and speech-understanding tests help distinguish conductive or central causes and guide rehabilitation. [p.1507]

WHO grades by PTA4 in the better-hearing ear: normal <20 dB; mild 20 to <35 dB; moderate 35 to <50 dB; moderately severe 50 to <65 dB; severe 65 to <80 dB; profound 80 to <95 dB; complete ≥95 dB. Mild loss may impair conversation in noise despite no difficulty with conversational speech in quiet; moderate loss may also cause difficulty in quiet. [p.1509, Table 2]

Management goals: improve communication, daily engagement and safety; no restorative therapy is available in this review. Reduce noise exposure and use hearing protection as needed. Converse face to face at arm’s length, reduce background noise and reverberation, and use visual facial/lip cues. Internet calls and closed captions are additional options at any hearing level. [p.1508–1509; p.1510, Figure 2]

Hearing aids are the primary treatment: amplification improves audibility; directional microphones and digital processing in more advanced devices improve the signal-to-noise ratio. The cited Cochrane review found improved hearing-specific and general health-related quality of life. Technologies cannot fully compensate for degraded peripheral sound encoding. [p.1508–1509; p.1511]

Over-the-counter (OTC) aids: FDA regulations effective October 17, 2022 allowed purchase without a hearing professional. Intended for adults with perceived mild-to-moderate loss, described in the text as PTA4 generally less than 60 dB, encompassing 90 to 95% of persons with hearing loss. Figure 2 lists 10–60 dB and describes PTA4 ≤60 dB; these are general usefulness ranges, not the WHO severity boundaries. [p.1509; p.1510, Figure 2]

Prescription aids: obtained through a hearing professional, with higher sound output for more severe loss. Figure 2 depicts a general PTA4 range of 20–90 dB while describing prescription aids as suitable for all levels of hearing loss. Communication strategies and everyday hearing technologies remain useful at any level. [p.1509–1510, Figure 2]

Cochlear implant referral: consider greater hearing loss (PTA4 generally ≥60 dB) with persistent difficulty understanding speech despite hearing aids; Figure 2 specifies ≥60 dB in one or both ears and insufficient benefit for daily communication. Refer to an implant center or an otolaryngologist specializing in implantation. The device directly stimulates the cochlear nerve; outpatient surgery takes approximately 2 hours and adaptation takes 6 to 12 months. Results vary. [p.1510, Figure 2; p.1511]

Dementia association: the 2020 Lancet Commission identified middle- and late-life hearing loss as the largest potentially modifiable dementia risk factor, accounting for 8% of cases. Proposed mechanisms involve cognitive load, brain atrophy and social isolation; these are hypotheses about the observed association. [p.1505–1506]

ACHIEVE: hearing intervention (hearing aids plus related audiologic support) versus health education in adults 70 to 84 years old with hearing loss did not reduce 3-year cognitive decline in the primary analysis of the total cohort. A prespecified sensitivity analysis in participants at increased baseline risk showed 48% less cognitive change over 3 years (global cognitive decline −0.211 SD units versus −0.402 SD units). No effect was found in healthy volunteers at decreased baseline risk. Longer follow-up is needed to clarify effects on cognitive decline and dementia risk. [p.1511]

Guidelines as reported in 2024: USPSTF 2021 found insufficient evidence to assess benefits and harms of screening asymptomatic adults 50 years or older. For symptoms or patient concerns, clinicians should use clinical judgment about hearing tests. The author knew of no other clinical practice guidelines on age-related hearing loss at publication. [p.1511]

Author’s approach to the vignette: exclude a conductive cause and indications for otolaryngology referral, then presume some age-related loss. Counsel the patient and spouse about communication, social functioning and potential cognitive-health effects. According to preference, offer an audiologist’s diagnostic evaluation/counseling or a well-regarded hearing-aid retailer; provide smartphone self-testing resources for technology-familiar patients and discuss OTC aids. The forecast of increasing OTC choices and support over the next 2 to 3 years is the author’s 2024 expectation. [p.1511–1512]

cards.title: AGS Beers Criteria 2023: medication risks and alternatives
cards.provenance: 1_AGS-Beers-2023.pdf; Alternative-Treatments-to-Selected-Medications-in-the-2023-American-Geriatrics-Society-Beers.pdf. Read from the supplied local files; page-cited paraphrases, not a replacement for the source.
bullets: Scope: adults aged 65 or older in ambulatory, acute and institutional care; hospice and end-of-life care are excluded. Use the criteria to inform shared decisions, with attention to the indication and individual circumstances. [p.2052]

Antipsychotics: bipolar disorder is among the approved-indication exceptions. Dementia-related behavior or delirium does not routinely justify treatment: first try appropriate non-drug measures; substantial danger to self or others is an exception, with periodic attempts to reduce treatment. [pp.2059–2060, Table 2]

Z-drugs give only small improvements in sleep latency and duration while carrying benzodiazepine-like adverse effects, including delirium, falls and fractures; the recommendation is to avoid them. [p.2060]

Clonazepam belongs to the benzodiazepines marked for avoidance: older adults are more sensitive, and all benzodiazepines increase cognitive impairment, delirium, falls, fractures and motor-vehicle crashes. The table allows selected indications; it does not rank this patient’s four drugs in a discontinuation sequence. [p.2060]

Paroxetine is among strongly anticholinergic antidepressants to avoid because of anticholinergic effects, sedation and orthostatic hypotension. This is the Beers basis relevant to 2024 Q94; the accepted serotonin-syndrome alternative is not established by that row. [p.2059]

Avoid scheduled PPI use beyond eight weeks unless there is a justified exception, such as high bleeding risk, erosive esophagitis, Barrett’s esophagitis, a hypersecretory disorder or demonstrated maintenance need. [p.2062]

For nonvalvular AF or VTE, avoid initiating warfarin when a suitable DOAC is available. Continuing established warfarin can be reasonable when INR control is good and adverse effects are absent; this is different from starting treatment. [p.2057]

For long-term AF or VTE treatment, prefer safer alternatives to rivaroxaban because of greater major and gastrointestinal bleeding risk, particularly compared with apixaban. Use caution with dabigatran; consider kidney function, indication and body weight when selecting and dosing a DOAC. [pp.2058,2064, Box 1]
Clonidine is not recommended for routine hypertension treatment because of CNS adverse effects, bradycardia and orthostatic hypotension; avoid it as first-line hypertension therapy. [p.2058]

Alternatives companion: assess the cause of insomnia and use CBT-I first. If medication is needed after other approaches, low-dose doxepin, ramelteon or an orexin antagonist may be safer alternatives; evidence for meaningful melatonin benefit is limited. [companion PDF pp.18–19]

Sulfonylureas: avoid as first- or second-line monotherapy or add-on treatment unless substantial barriers prevent use of safer, more effective agents; if one is used, prefer a short-acting agent such as glipizide over glyburide or glimepiride. Strong recommendation; evidence: hypoglycemia high, cardiovascular events/all-cause mortality moderate, cardiovascular death/ischemic stroke low. [AGS Beers 2023, Table 2, p.2061]

Dextromethorphan/quinidine: avoid in heart failure (strong recommendation, low-quality evidence). Separately, use with caution: efficacy is limited for dementia-related behavioral symptoms (this efficacy qualification does not apply to pseudobulbar affect), with falls, important interactions and heart-failure concerns (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). [AGS Beers 2023, Table 3, p.2065; Table 4, p.2068]

Opioids: avoid in older adults with delirium or high delirium risk because they can induce or worsen delirium, with the table rationale qualifying this advice. For pain, balance treatment using validated pain assessment and multimodal approaches, including nondrug measures, to minimize opioid use. Strong recommendation; moderate-quality evidence. [AGS Beers 2023, Table 3, p.2066]

Anticholinergics: in people with prior falls or fractures, avoid unless safer alternatives are unavailable; if a listed drug must be used, consider reducing other CNS-active drugs and implement fall-risk reduction strategies. Strong recommendation; high-quality evidence for anticholinergics. [AGS Beers 2023, Table 3, p.2066]

Estrogen: do not start systemic oral or transdermal estrogen; consider deprescribing existing systemic treatment (strong recommendation, high-quality evidence). Low-dose vaginal cream/tablets are acceptable for dyspareunia, recurrent lower UTIs and other vaginal symptoms (weak recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). After breast cancer, if nonhormonal measures fail, discuss low-dose vaginal estrogen risks and benefits with the healthcare provider. [AGS Beers 2023, Table 2, p.2061]

Muscle relaxants: avoidance for agents typically used for musculoskeletal complaints does not apply to the spasticity agents baclofen and tizanidine, which can still cause substantial adverse effects. The musculoskeletal-relaxant avoidance is strong, with moderate-quality evidence. [AGS Beers 2023, Table 2, p.2063]

Baclofen: avoid in older adults with eGFR <60 mL/min because encephalopathy requiring hospitalization is more likely; if it cannot be avoided, use the lowest effective dose and monitor for CNS toxicity, including altered mental status. Strong recommendation; moderate-quality evidence. [AGS Beers 2023, Table 6, p.2073]

Sodium: use mirtazapine, SNRIs, SSRIs, TCAs, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, antipsychotics, diuretics and tramadol with caution; these can cause or worsen SIADH/hyponatremia, so monitor sodium closely when starting or changing doses. Strong recommendation; moderate-quality evidence. [AGS Beers 2023, Table 4, p.2068]

CNS combinations: avoid concurrent use of 3 or more drugs from these CNS-active groups and minimize their number: antiepileptics including gabapentinoids, antidepressants (TCAs, SSRIs, SNRIs), antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, Z-drugs, opioids and skeletal muscle relaxants, because of falls and fractures. Strong recommendation; high-quality evidence. [AGS Beers 2023, Table 5, p.2070]

cards.title: Stroke Rehabilitation Clinician Handbook 2020: clinical consequences (chapter 1)
cards.provenance: Chapter 1_Clinical Consequences_0.pdf. Read from the supplied local files; page-cited paraphrases, not a replacement for the source.
bullets: ACA infarction typically causes contralateral weakness and sensory loss affecting the leg more than the arm; abulia, urinary incontinence and gait apraxia can accompany it. The ACA point tested in 2023 Q76 is on chapter page 6, although that reference row says page 17. [PDF p.6]

MCA infarction more prominently affects face and arm. Motor and sensory loss and homonymous hemianopsia are contralateral; left-hemisphere lesions may produce aphasia, whereas right-hemisphere lesions may produce left neglect. [chapter pp.6–7]

Neglect is failure to respond or orient to stimuli on the side opposite the lesion. Right-hemisphere stroke commonly produces left-sided neglect; it can affect eating, dressing and navigation and is associated with worse functional recovery. [PDF p.9]

Broca/nonfluent aphasia combines effortful, reduced verbal output with relatively preserved comprehension and poor repetition. This pattern matches the comprehension/output/repetition features tested in 2023 Q5 and 2024 Q48. [chapter pp.11–12]

Use fluency, comprehension and repetition together: impaired repetition also occurs in conduction aphasia, where speech remains fluent and comprehension is good. Preserved repetition separates transcortical motor aphasia from Broca aphasia. [PDF p.11]

Apraxia is inability to carry out purposeful learned activity despite adequate strength, mobility, sensation, coordination and comprehension. Left-hemisphere lesions can cause it; preserved understanding with difficulty executing dressing or tool-use actions is the distinction tested in 2024 Q36. [PDF p.15]

Abducens palsy with contralateral hemiparesis localizes to the lower pons in the handbook’s Raymond syndrome entry. The crossed cranial-nerve/limb pattern distinguishes it from the listed midbrain and medullary syndromes. [PDF p.17]

cards.title: Lancet Commission 2024: dementia prevention, intervention and care
cards.provenance: lancet2024.pdf. Read from the supplied local files; page-cited paraphrases, not a replacement for the source.
bullets: The 2024 model adds high LDL cholesterol and untreated vision loss to the previous twelve factors. Its combined population-attributable fraction is about 45%; this is a model of potentially modifiable risk, not a demonstrated reduction of over 60% from an intervention. [PDF p.23]

The commission recommends making hearing aids accessible. ACHIEVE found no overall benefit on its three-year cognition endpoint, but the higher-risk ARIC subgroup had less cognitive decline. Observational associations with less dementia should be distinguished from a trial proving dementia prevention. [PDF pp.2,10]

Smoking cessation is supported: compared with continuing smokers, former smokers had lower risk in the reviewed cohorts. The 2024 model now treats smoking as a midlife risk factor; the report describes cessation as beneficial, while age-specific results vary. [PDF p.13]

Treat hypertension: two meta-analyses of randomized trials found protective effects on cognition or dementia; a shorter-duration analysis did not establish a dementia-incidence effect. The commission recommends preventing or reducing hypertension across midlife. [PDF pp.2,16–17]

For the midlife-risk comparison tested in 2023 Q56, the 2024 model assigns hearing loss a weighted attributable fraction of 7%, versus about 3% for traumatic brain injury, 2% for hypertension and 1% for obesity. These are population fractions, not an individual’s probability. [PDF p.23, Table 1]

2025 Q61 official key: the option asserting that APOE ε4 risk cannot be reduced by external intervention (IMA final answer key, June 2025, Q61, option א). The cited 2024 report instead explicitly says risk remains modifiable regardless of APOE genetic status and that multicomponent approaches may benefit both higher- and lower-genetic-risk groups. The official key is preserved. [PDF p.2]

cards.title: ADA Standards of Care 2026: Older Adults (section 13)
cards.provenance: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026 ADA.pdf. Read from the supplied local files; page-cited paraphrases, not a replacement for the source.
bullets: Assess medical, psychological, functional and social circumstances together. Screen at least annually for geriatric syndromes, hypoglycemia and polypharmacy; screen for cognitive impairment at age 65 or older at the initial visit, annually and as appropriate. [pp.S277–S278]

For an older adult with few stable illnesses and intact cognition/function, a reasonable A1C goal is below 7.0–7.5%. Table 13.2 gives fasting/premeal glucose 80–130 mg/dL and blood pressure below 130/80 mmHg; goals are individualized. [p.S284, Table 13.2]

For complex/intermediate health, Table 13.2 gives a less stringent A1C goal below 8.0% and fasting/premeal glucose 90–150 mg/dL. Cognitive or functional limitations, frailty, treatment risks and patient preferences guide individualization. [p.S284, Table 13.2]

For very complex/poor health, avoid reliance on A1C. Focus on preventing hypoglycemia and symptomatic hyperglycemia; Table 13.2 gives fasting/premeal glucose 100–180 mg/dL. This differs from the older exam option that couples this range with A1C below 8.5%. [p.S284, Table 13.2]

When treatment burdens or harms exceed benefits, deintensify within individualized goals; simplify complex insulin plans to reduce hypoglycemia, polypharmacy and burden. Cardiovascular- and kidney-protective agents remain relevant in patients with the corresponding risks, irrespective of glycemia. [p.S285, recommendations 13.14a–d]

Once-daily basal insulin may be reasonable for many older adults. Noninsulin options are generally preferred for their lower hypoglycemia risk and other benefits; select the regimen for the person’s ability, support and goals rather than leaving symptomatic hyperglycemia untreated. [p.S288]

Figure 13.3 permits discontinuing prandial insulin at doses of 10 units or less per dose and adding noninsulin treatment; drug choice depends on comorbidities and characteristics. DPP-4 inhibitors are listed among the possible noninsulin agents; they are not the only option. [p.S289, Figure 13.3]

cards.title: Advanced Dementia: Mitchell, NEJM 2015
cards.provenance: Mitchell-2015.pdf. Read from the supplied local files; page-cited paraphrases, not a replacement for the source.
bullets: Advanced dementia involves profound cognitive deficits, minimal speech, loss of independent ambulation and dependence in daily activities. Eating problems and infections are the common clinical complications that repeatedly require care decisions. [p.2534]

The hospice guideline in Table 1 requires at least FAST 7c with all features from 6a through 7c, plus a qualifying medical complication in the preceding year. FAST 7c means inability to walk independently; inability to sit, smile or hold the head occurs in later stages. [p.2535, Table 1]

The nutritional complication in Table 1 is insufficient food or fluid to sustain life; in tube-fed patients the listed markers are weight loss over 10% in six months or albumin below 2.5 g/dL. These contextual criteria explain the components tested in 2020 Q16 and 2024 Q57; one isolated marker does not establish every eligibility requirement. [p.2535, Table 1]

Other qualifying complications include aspiration pneumonia, upper urinary infection, septicemia, recurrent fever despite antibiotics and multiple stage 3 or 4 pressure ulcers. Prognosis is uncertain: the article cautions that hospice criteria do not reliably predict six-month survival. [pp.2533–2535, Table 1]

Antimicrobials for pneumonia were associated with longer survival but greater discomfort in the observational CASCADE data. No randomized trials established survival or symptom benefit; the decision should follow the person’s goal of comfort or life prolongation and minimize treatment burden. [p.2537]

For persistent eating difficulty, hand feeding aims at comfort and interaction. Observational evidence does not establish tube-feeding benefits for survival or aspiration prevention; advance planning and shared decisions should align care with the patient’s wishes and goals. [pp.2534–2536]

cards.title: Management of Acute Hip Fracture: NEJM 2017, with 2018 correspondence
cards.provenance: Bhandari M, Swiontkowski M. NEJM 2017;377:2053–2062; correspondence, NEJM 2018;378:971–972. Read from the supplied PDFs; page-cited paraphrases. The review is primary; correspondence is second-tier.
bullets: Garden I–II are nondisplaced or impacted femoral-neck patterns; the review selects internal fixation for nondisplaced fractures. A basicervical or vertically oriented line favors a sliding hip screw rather than multiple cancellous screws. [pp.2053–2054, 2057; Fig.3 p.2056]

For a displaced femoral-neck fragility fracture in an older adult, arthroplasty is generally preferred. The algorithm chooses total replacement for a healthy, cognitively intact independent walker and hemiarthroplasty when cognition or ambulation is limited. [pp.2056, 2059; Fig.3]

Total hip arthroplasty produced better hip-function ratings than hemiarthroplasty over 12–48 months, but more dislocations. The lower pooled reoperation risk was driven mainly by trials without concealed treatment allocation. [p.2059]

Stable intertrochanteric fractures can be fixed with a sliding hip screw; unstable patterns with a large posteromedial fragment or a reverse-oblique line favor an intramedullary nail. Subtrochanteric fractures usually receive an intramedullary nail. [pp.2056, 2059–2060; Fig.3]

The images in 2020 Q25 and Q57 match Figure 2B (displaced femoral neck) and Figure 2E (subtrochanteric) respectively. Applying the algorithm yields arthroplasty for Q25 and an intramedullary nail for Q57. [pp.2055–2056, Figs.2–3]

Guidelines summarized in the review recommend surgery within 48 hours of the event. Its observational meta-analysis associates surgery within 24 hours of admission with lower mortality, while warning that sicker patients are more likely to have delayed surgery. [p.2057]

Early mobilization and multidisciplinary geriatric care support recovery; perioperative care also includes thromboprophylaxis, antibiotic prophylaxis and osteoporosis assessment and treatment. [p.2060]

2022-Jun Q82 official key: surgery within 24 hours (IMA final key, Q82, p.3). Review: earlier surgery is associated with lower mortality, and prompt bisphosphonate treatment is encouraged to reduce subsequent fractures. Correspondence (Anagnostis et al.): the cited mortality benefit specifically concerns intravenous zoledronic acid given 2–12 weeks after fracture, compared with placebo; it is not a class-wide claim for every dose in the first month. [Review pp.2057, 2060; correspondence p.971]

cards.title: AGS Choosing Wisely: Ten Things Physicians and Patients Should Question (2013–2014)
cards.provenance: AGS-Choosing-Wisely-Ten-Things-2014.pdf; items 1–5 released 21 February 2013, items 6–10 on 27 February 2014. This card summarizes the historical list cited by the papers, not a later revision.
bullets: In advanced dementia, offer assisted oral feeding instead of percutaneous feeding tubes. Careful hand feeding is at least as good for death, aspiration pneumonia, functional status and comfort. [PDF p.1, item 1]
Tube feeding is associated with agitation, greater use of physical and chemical restraints, and worsening pressure ulcers. This is the association tested in 2020 Q42. [PDF p.1, item 1]

For anorexia or cachexia in older adults, the list favors social support, feeding assistance and discussion of goals over prescription appetite stimulants or high-calorie supplements. Weight gain with supplements does not establish improved quality of life, mood, function or survival. [PDF p.2, item 8]

Megestrol offers little appetite or weight benefit, without improved survival or quality of life, and increases thrombotic events, fluid retention and death. Evidence for mirtazapine as an appetite or weight treatment without depression is limited. [PDF p.2, item 8]

Review the drug regimen before prescribing: identify high-risk medicines, interactions and treatments continued beyond their indication. This provides the medication-review context for Q92; item 8 does not explicitly instruct stopping appetite-suppressing medicines. [PDF p.2, items 8–9]

cards.title: ESC/EACTS 2025 valvular heart disease
cards.editionNotice: Additional reading: this guideline is not named in IMA P005-2026. Official exam text, sources and keys remain unchanged.
cards.provenance: Own-word summaries from the supplied PDF, checked against rendered recommendation tables and pages. Recommendation class/evidence level are given where the source grades the statement; definitions and narrative follow-up are marked ungraded.
bullets: Scope: additional current-practice reading, not the Hazzard book and not a P005-2026 required article. Definitions and follow-up prose below have no separate recommendation class or evidence level.

AS severity: high-gradient severe AS has mean gradient >=40 mmHg, Vmax >=4.0 m/s and AVA <=1.0 cm2 (or <=0.6 cm2/m2); low flow is SVi <=35 mL/m2. With discordant measurements, confirm severity using integrated imaging rather than AVA alone. [Definition; section 8.2.1, p4663 / PDF p29]

Severe AS: intervene for symptoms with high-gradient disease, or confirmed low-flow/low-gradient disease and LVEF <50% [I/B]; with preserved LVEF, confirmed symptomatic low-flow/low-gradient AS merits consideration [IIa/B]. [Recommendation Table 4, p4670 / PDF p36]

Asymptomatic severe AS: intervene when LVEF <50% without another cause [I/B]. In severe high-gradient AS with LVEF >=50%, normal exercise testing if feasible and low procedural risk, early intervention is an alternative to close surveillance [IIa/A]. This broad early-intervention option differs from ACC/AHA 2020. [Recommendation Table 4, p4670 / PDF p36]

Additional asymptomatic AS triggers at low procedural risk include mean gradient >=60 mmHg or Vmax >5.0 m/s; severe calcification with Vmax progression >=0.3 m/s/year; repeatedly >3 times age/sex-adjusted normal BNP/NT-proBNP without another explanation; or LVEF <55% without another cause [IIa/B]. Sustained exercise BP fall >20 mmHg is IIa/C. [Recommendation Table 4, p4670 / PDF p36]

TAVI versus SAVR: TAVI is recommended from age 70 with a tricuspid aortic valve and suitable anatomy [I/A]; SAVR is recommended below 70 when surgical risk is low [I/B]. Other patients need an individual Heart Team choice incorporating anatomy, lifetime valve strategy, life expectancy and preference [I/C]. These age boundaries differ from ACC/AHA's <65, 65-80 and >80 framework. [Recommendation Table 4, p4670 / PDF p36]

AR severity uses integrated findings: vena contracta >6 mm, EROA >=30 mm2, regurgitant volume >=60 mL/beat and echo regurgitant fraction >50%; holodiastolic descending-aortic reversal and LV consequences support the assessment. [Definition; Figure 4, p4659 / PDF p25]

Severe AR: surgery is recommended for symptoms regardless of LV function, or without symptoms if resting LVEF <=50%, LVESD >50 mm or LVESDi >25 mm/m2 [I/B]. The indexed threshold is especially relevant in small adults. ACC/AHA 2020 uses LVEF <=55% for its class 1 indication. [Recommendation Table 3, p4662 / PDF p28]

Earlier surgery in asymptomatic severe AR may be considered at low surgical risk if LVEF <=55%, LVESDi >22 mm/m2 or LVESVi >45 mL/m2 [IIb/B]. TAVI may be considered for symptomatic severe AR when surgery is unsuitable and anatomy is suitable [IIb/B]. [Recommendation Table 3, p4662 / PDF p28]

MR severity: vena contracta >=7 mm (>=8 mm biplane), EROA >=40 mm2 and regurgitant volume >=60 mL support severe MR; in secondary MR, an elliptical orifice or low-flow state can justify lower thresholds, with EROA >=30 mm2 or regurgitant volume >=45 mL associated with important outcomes. Regurgitant fraction >=50% is another criterion. Integrate findings and distinguish primary from ventricular or atrial secondary MR. [Definition; Figure 10, p4672 / PDF p38]

Severe primary MR: repair is preferred when durable [I/B]; surgery is recommended for operable symptomatic patients or asymptomatic LV dysfunction, defined by LVEF <=60%, LVESD >=40 mm or LVESDi >=20 mm/m2 [I/B]. [Recommendation Table 6, p4674 / PDF p40]

With preserved LV function, low-risk asymptomatic severe primary MR warrants durable repair if at least three are present: AF, resting SPAP >50 mmHg, LA volume index >=60 mL/m2 or diameter >=55 mm, and at least moderate secondary TR [I/B]. AF secondary to MR or pulmonary hypertension supports consideration of surgery; major LA enlargement supports repair in a low-risk patient at a Heart Valve Centre when a durable result is likely [IIa/B]. [Recommendation Table 6, p4675 / PDF p41]

For symptomatic severe primary MR with suitable anatomy and high surgical risk, TEER should be considered [IIa/B]. This is a Heart Team decision, not an age-only rule. [Recommendation Table 6, p4675 / PDF p41]

Ventricular secondary MR: after optimized GDMT and CRT when indicated, TEER is recommended in stable symptomatic patients with impaired LVEF (<50% in the recommendation) and without relevant CAD who meet the clinical/echo selection criteria [I/A]. Key Table 7 criteria include NYHA >=II, LVEF 20%-50%, LVESD <=70 mm and SPAP <=70 mmHg; exclude severe RV dysfunction, advanced HF and other major valve disease, and require suitable anatomy plus an HF admission in the previous year or BNP >=300 pg/mL / NT-proBNP >=1000 pg/mL. ACC/AHA 2020 grades selected secondary-MR TEER 2a. [Recommendation Table 7 and Table 7, pp4678-4679 / PDF pp44-45]
Mechanical valves require lifelong VKA [I/A]; DOACs and/or DAPT must not replace it to prevent valve thrombosis [III/A]. [Recommendation Table 14, p4693 / PDF p59]

Standard mechanical-valve INR targets: current-generation bileaflet or single-tilting aortic valve without extra prothrombotic factors, 2.5 (range 2-3); with such factors, 3.0 (2.5-3.5). Older ball-cage/tilting-disc valves and any mitral/tricuspid mechanical valve: 3.0 (2.5-3.5) without extra factors, 3.5 (3-4) with them. Targets depend on valve type/position and patient risk [I/A]; the table footnote allows INR 2.0 (1.5-2.5) for the current-generation aortic group at high bleeding risk. [Table 10 and Recommendation Table 14, p4693 / PDF p59]

Adding aspirin 75-100 mg/day to VKA is considered for selected mechanical-valve patients with concomitant symptomatic atherosclerotic disease after individual bleeding-risk assessment [IIa/B]; it is not routine. Separately, major thromboembolism despite adequate INR may justify increasing the INR target or adding low-dose aspirin [IIa/C]. ACC/AHA's separate-antiplatelet-indication recommendation is class 2b. [Recommendation Table 14, p4693 / PDF p59]

After surgical bioprosthetic implantation without another OAC indication: aortic position, aspirin 75-100 mg/day or VKA for the first 3 months [IIa/B]; mitral/tricuspid position, VKA for the first 3 months [IIa/B]. [Recommendation Table 16, p4696 / PDF p62]

After TAVI without another OAC indication: aspirin 75-100 mg/day for 12 months [I/A], then consider continued low-dose aspirin [IIa/C]. DAPT without a separate clear indication is not recommended [III/B], and routine OAC is not recommended [III/A]. This differs from optional short DAPT/VKA strategies in ACC/AHA 2020. [Recommendation Table 16, p4696 / PDF p62]

With a separate OAC indication after surgical bioprosthetic implantation, continue OAC [I/B]; in AF, DOACs should be considered over VKA after 3 months [IIa/B]. TAVI patients with another OAC indication require OAC [I/B]. These rules do not apply to mechanical valves. [Recommendation Table 16, pp4696-4697 / PDF pp62-63]

Endocarditis prevention: dental extraction/oral surgery and gingival or periapical manipulation warrant prophylaxis in patients with prosthetic valves (including transcatheter), prosthetic repair material or previous IE; also consider it after transcatheter mitral/tricuspid repair. Stress dental/skin hygiene and asepsis. The VHD text refers to the separate ESC endocarditis guideline for regimen details. [Ungraded narrative; section 14.4.3, p4698 / PDF p64]

Native-valve follow-up: severe asymptomatic AS at least every 6 months, moderate degenerative AS at least yearly; severe asymptomatic AR yearly, or every 3-6 months near intervention thresholds/progressive LV changes; moderate AR yearly clinically with echo every 2 years. [Ungraded follow-up; sections 7.5 and 8.6, pp4660,4671 / PDF pp26,37]

MR/prosthesis follow-up: severe asymptomatic primary MR without an intervention indication, clinical and echo review twice yearly; moderate MR with preserved LV function, yearly clinical review and echo every 1-2 years. Bioprosthetic valves need a baseline TTE within 3 months, again at 1 year and annually thereafter, sooner for symptoms. [Ungraded follow-up; sections 9.1.5 and 14.2, pp4675,4691 / PDF pp41,57]

Older-adult assessment: frailty, nutrition, comorbidity, functional recovery, life expectancy and the patient's goals supplement procedural risk scores. Surgical scores can overestimate TAVI risk. Frailty is assessed systematically with appropriate tools; decisions remain multidisciplinary and patient-centred. [Ungraded assessment; sections 5.1-5.2 and Figure 3, pp4653-4654 / PDF pp19-20]

cards.title: ACC/AHA 2020 valvular heart disease (with 2021-2024 corrections)
cards.editionNotice: Additional reading: this guideline is not named in IMA P005-2026. Official exam text, sources and keys remain unchanged.
cards.provenance: Own-word summaries from the supplied PDF, checked against rendered recommendation tables and pages. Recommendation class/evidence level are given where the source grades the statement; definitions and narrative follow-up are marked ungraded.
bullets: Scope: additional current-practice reading, not the Hazzard book and not a P005-2026 required article. This card applies the supplied 2021, 2023 and 2024 corrections; classes below are those of ACC/AHA 2020, not upgrades from newer ESC guidance.

Severe AS: Vmax >=4 m/s or mean gradient >=40 mmHg; AVA is typically <=1.0 cm2 but is not required for the high-gradient definition. Low-flow/low-gradient phenotypes require additional confirmation; preserved-EF low-flow AS uses SVi <35 mL/m2 at systolic BP <140 mmHg. [Definition; Table 13, e91 / PDF p20]

AS intervention: symptomatic high-gradient severe AS warrants AVR [1/A]; asymptomatic severe AS with LVEF <50%, severe AS at other cardiac surgery, or symptomatic low-flow/low-gradient AS with reduced EF warrants AVR [1/B-NR]. With preserved EF and low-flow/low-gradient AS, AS must be the most likely cause of symptoms [1/B-NR]. [Section 3.2.3, e94 / PDF p23]

Asymptomatic severe AS at low surgical risk: reduced exercise tolerance normalized for age and sex or exercise systolic BP fall >=10 mmHg [2a/B-NR]; Vmax >=5 m/s [2a/B-R]; BNP >3 times normal or Vmax increase >=0.3 m/s/year [2a/B-NR] support AVR. ESC 2025 also offers early intervention more broadly in low-risk high-gradient severe AS with preserved EF. [Section 3.2.3, e94 / PDF p23]

TAVI versus SAVR when a bioprosthetic AVR is appropriate: below 65 years or expected survival >20 years, SAVR [1/A]; symptomatic patients aged 65-80 with feasible transfemoral access, either SAVR or TAVI after shared decision-making [1/A]; symptomatic patients above 80 or with expected survival <10 years, transfemoral TAVI if feasible [1/A]. ESC 2025 instead uses a 70-year boundary for suitable tricuspid-valve AS. [Section 3.2.4.2, e99 / PDF p28]

High/prohibitive surgical-risk severe symptomatic AS: TAVI is recommended only when expected survival after TAVI exceeds 12 months with acceptable quality of life [1/A]. Predicted survival <12 months or minimal expected quality-of-life gain supports palliative care after shared decision-making [1/C-EO]. [Section 3.2.4.2, e99 / PDF p28]

Severe AR: vena contracta >0.6 cm, regurgitant volume >=60 mL/beat, regurgitant fraction >=50% or ERO >=0.3 cm2 are major criteria; chronic severe AR also requires evidence of LV dilation. Integrate the measurements rather than use a single cutoff. [Definition; Table 15, e105 / PDF p34]

Severe AR: operate for symptoms regardless of LV function, or without symptoms when LVEF <=55% and no other explanation for LV dysfunction [1/B-NR]. With LVEF >55%, LVESD >50 mm or indexed LVESD >25 mm/m2 makes surgery reasonable [2a/B-NR]. ESC 2025's class I LVEF threshold is <=50%. [Section 4.3.3, e107 / PDF p36]

Asymptomatic severe AR at low surgical risk: a progressive LVEF decline to 55%-60% across at least 3 studies, or increasing LVEDD into the >65 mm range, may justify surgery [2b/B-NR]. TAVI should not replace indicated SAVR in an operable patient with isolated severe AR [3: Harm/B-NR]. [Section 4.3.3, e107 / PDF p36]

Severe primary MR: vena contracta >=0.7 cm, regurgitant volume >=60 mL, regurgitant fraction >=50% and ERO >=0.40 cm2 are integrated severity criteria; not every criterion is present in every patient. [Definition; Table 17, e121 / PDF p50]

Primary MR: symptomatic severe disease warrants mitral-valve intervention [1/B-NR]; asymptomatic severe disease with LVEF <=60% and/or LVESD >=40 mm warrants surgery [1/B-NR]. Prefer repair over replacement for degenerative disease when a durable repair is achievable [1/B-NR]. [Section 7.2.4 and Table 17, e121,e124 / PDF pp50,53]

Asymptomatic severe primary MR with LVEF >60% and LVESD <40 mm: repair is reasonable at an expert valve centre if durable success is >95% and expected mortality <1% [2a/B-NR]. In severely symptomatic primary MR at high/prohibitive surgical risk, TEER is reasonable with favourable anatomy and life expectancy >=1 year [2a/B-NR]. [Section 7.2.4, e124 / PDF p53]

Secondary MR despite optimal HF therapy: TEER is reasonable with persistent NYHA II-IV symptoms, suitable TEE anatomy, LVEF 20%-50%, LVESD <=70 mm and PASP <=70 mmHg [2a/B-R]. The 2021 correction specifies LVESD, not LVEDD. ESC 2025 grades its selected ventricular-SMR TEER indication I/A. [Section 7.3.4, e129 / PDF p58; 2021 correction e229]

Mechanical valves: use VKA [1/A]. Target INR 2.5 for a current bileaflet/single-tilting aortic valve without thromboembolic risk factors; 3.0 for mechanical mitral valves or aortic valves with additional risk factors/older-generation prostheses [1/B-NR]. [Section 11.2, e142 / PDF p71]

Mechanical valve plus a separate antiplatelet indication: aspirin 75-100 mg/day may be added to VKA only when bleeding risk is low [2b/B-R]; routine aspirin is not implied. ESC 2025 specifies symptomatic atherosclerotic disease and grades that selected use IIa/B. [Section 11.2 recommendation 8, e142 / PDF p71]

Mechanical On-X aortic valve without thromboembolic risk factors: INR 1.5-2.0 with continued aspirin 75-100 mg/day may be reasonable starting at least 3 months after surgery [2b/B-R]; do not generalize this to all mechanical valves. [Section 11.2 recommendation 9, e142 / PDF p71]

DOAC limits: dabigatran is contraindicated in mechanical valves [3: Harm/B-R]; anti-Xa oral anticoagulants are not recommended in mechanical valves [3: Harm/C-EO]. Rivaroxaban 10 mg/day plus aspirin after TAVI without another OAC indication is contraindicated [3: Harm/B-R]. [Section 11.2 recommendations 12-14, e142 / PDF p71]

Bioprostheses without another OAC indication: aspirin 75-100 mg/day is reasonable after TAVI [2a/B-R] or surgical AVR/mitral replacement [2a/B-NR]. At low bleeding risk after surgical AVR/mitral replacement, VKA with INR 2.5 for 3-6 months is reasonable [2a/B-NR]. [Section 11.2, e142 / PDF p71]

The 2020 document also permits 3-6 months of DAPT after TAVI [2b/B-NR] or at least 3 months of VKA at INR 2.5 [2b/B-NR] in low-bleeding-risk patients. These are older options: ESC 2025 recommends aspirin alone without another indication and advises against routine DAPT/OAC. [Section 11.2, e142 / PDF p71; compare ESC Recommendation Table 16]

IE prophylaxis is reasonable before dental procedures manipulating gingiva/periapical tissue or perforating oral mucosa for prosthetic valves, prosthetic repair material, previous IE, specified cyanotic/residual congenital lesions, or transplant valvulopathy [2a/C-LD]. Routine prophylaxis for nondental procedures without active infection is not recommended [3: No Benefit/B-NR]. [Section 2.4.2, e82 / PDF p11]

Imaging/follow-up: TTE is the standard initial test; investigate discordant findings with additional imaging. With normal LV function and no symptoms, mild AS/AR/MR generally needs echo every 3-5 years, moderate disease every 1-2 years and severe disease every 6-12 months; use earlier reassessment for LV dilation, mixed lesions or new symptoms. [Ungraded general guidance; Tables 3,5, e80-e81 / PDF pp9-10]

Prosthetic valves: obtain a postprocedural TTE baseline [1/B-NR]; new symptoms/signs require repeat TTE [1/C-EO] and, when dysfunction is suspected, TEE/CT/fluoroscopy even if TTE is unrevealing [1/C-LD]. Surgical bioprosthetic TTE at 5 and 10 years then annually is reasonable [2a/C-LD]. [Section 11.1.1, e137 / PDF p66]

Risk and frailty: estimate procedure-specific risk and discuss it with the patient [1/C-EO]. Frailty, irreversible organ dysfunction and procedural impediments supplement STS estimates. Corrected Table 8 uses >50% death/major morbidity at 30 days for prohibitive risk; its corrected high-risk frailty cell reads <=1 index with moderate-to-severe frailty. [Section 2.5, e85 / PDF p14; 2023 e8 and 2024 e267 corrections]

Correction detail: secondary rheumatic-fever prophylaxis is distinct from dental IE prophylaxis; Table 6's penicillin V dose is 250 mg orally twice daily after the 2023 correction. This is a table regimen, not a new IE-prophylaxis dose. [Section 2.4.1: 1/C-EO; Table 6, e82 / PDF p11; 2023 e185 correction]
